sections.heading: CHARACTERS
sections.text: Characters include all beings in the game world, from the Heroes run by the players to the Villains, Foes, Minions, and Extras run by the GM. They include not only sentient beings but also animals, monsters, mindless undead, unthinking robots, career politicians, and so on. This chapter discusses the kinds of characters in the game and the characteristics used to describe them. It also provides rules for creating Heroes and having them develop and become

sections.heading: CHARACTER TYPES
sections.text: There are five types of characters: Heroes, Villains, Foes, Minions, and Extras. Heroes are the characters run by the players. The GM runs all other characters, so they’re sometimes called nonplayer characters or NPCs. Villains are the super-powered adversaries whose diabolical schemes the Heroes spend their time trying to thwart. Foes are lesser enemies, characters important or powerful enough to merit individualized attention, but not enough to make them true Villains. They typically serve archvillains as henchmen and henchwomen, but usually report to the archvillain’s lieutenants, who are often Villains in their own right. Minions are the nameless foot soldiers who attack Heroes in groups and get knocked around like tenpins when the Heroes run out of bubblegum. Last are Extras, characters who could be allies, enemies, or something else entirely.

sections.heading: HEROES
sections.text: Heroes are defined by the following characteristics: Abilities, Talents, Powers, Perks, and Flaws. These characteristics are more than just descriptive. Each plays a mechanical role in the game and is discussed in greater detail later in this chapter. Heroes also possess narrative elements that help turn a collection of stats into a three-dimensional character. Most of this chapter discusses the process of creating Heroes (and other characters) and the options available when doing so.

sections.heading: VILLAINS
sections.text: Most Villains are defined by the same characteristics as Heroes: Abilities, Talents, Powers, Perks, and Flaws. Some Villains aren’t important or intelligent enough to have Talents, but otherwise Villains and Heroes have identical characteristics. As discussed later in this chapter, Villains are created much like Heroes, but the process is easier because it doesn’t involve any bookkeeping. Like Heroes, Villains have their own narrative elements that describe who they are, what they want, and so on. However, these elements differ from those used for Heroes. This is covered in Chapter 9. more capable over time.

sections.heading: FOES
sections.text: Foes are lesser enemies that often serve as henchmen, lieutenants, and elite soldiers. They’re created just like Villains and defined by the same characteristics and narrative elements. However, because these characters haven’t quite made it to the big leagues, Foes have only half as much Health as ordinary Heroes and Villains, making them more vulnerable to damage and special effects.

sections.heading: MINIONS
sections.text: As nameless foot soldiers whose primary role is to fight the Heroes en masse, Minions have only one characteristic: Threat. Threat indicates how dangerous these characters are, and is used when making attack rolls, defense rolls, and other combatrelated challenge rolls. Minions use only half their Threat when making challenge rolls to detect something, figure something out, or otherwise deal with situations beyond their usual purview. Although some Minions carry special gear or possess unique abilities, these things are always handled narratively. Creating Minions is as easy as it gets. All the GM has to do is assign a Threat rank, determine how many Minions there are, and note any unique characteristics they possess. When dealing with Minions, every member of the group has the same Threat. That’s why they’re Minions. Use the Threat Ranks table and the unique characteristics that follow as guidelines when creating these characters.

sections.heading: THREAT RANKS — DESCRIPTION THREAT
sections.text: Civilians 2d Bruisers 3d Professionals 4d Elites 5d Enhanced 6d Super 7d or More The following unique characteristics are common among comic book Minions. As noted above, they’re just guidelines. Feel free to create your own shorthand for your Minions. Animals: The Minions are animals. They have enhanced senses, can move faster than ordinary human beings, and/or possess whatever other special abilities make sense for that animal. Automatons: The Minions possess the Inanimate (Mindless) Power. Shooters: The Minions can attack enemies within Distant Range. Unique: The Minions have unique abilities like enhanced senses or flight that would be represented by separate Powers if these characters were Heroes or Villains. In this case, simply describe what they can do.

sections.heading: EXTRAS
sections.text: Any character run by the GM who isn’t a Villain, Foe, or Minion is an Extra. These characters cover a wide range in terms of who they are and how important they are to the game. Extras expected to get involved in the action—whether as allies, enemies, or unaffiliated third parties—should be created and handled like Villains or Foes, depending on how powerful you want them to be. On the other hand, Extras who only serve a narrative role in the game only need to be described in narrative terms. You don’t need stat blocks for a Hero’s boss or their spouse, much less for the nameless civilians who act as window dressing for the game world and victim-fodder for the Villains. If an unimportant nobody of an Extra suddenly becomes important in the middle of a game because the situation demands it or the players took a shine to them, the GM can stat the character up at that time.

sections.heading: CHARACTER CREATION
sections.text: The steps to creating characters other than Minions are provided below. Steps 2, 5, and 6 vary depending on whether you are creating a Hero, Villain, Foe, or Extra. As noted above, Minions are simple characters who only have a Threat rank, so these rules don’t apply to them. Step 1: Concept� Come up with a basic idea for the character. If you can’t think of anything, try the time-honored tradition of stealing your idea. There are enough out there that finding one you like shouldn’t be too difficult. You can create a carbon copy or mine what you find for inspiration. Step 2: Characteristics� When creating a Hero, spend Hero Points to buy your Abilities, Talents, Powers, and Perks. The GM will tell you how many Hero Points you can spend and the maximum Trait rank you can have, depending on the game’s power level (as discussed below). You should also select Flaws; you must have at least one Flaw and can have as many as three to start. When creating a Villain, Foe, or Extra, simply give them whatever Abilities, Talents, Powers, Perks, and Flaws you consider appropriate. GMs don’t have to worry about spending Hero Points or staying within the game’s power level and can give these characters as many Flaws as they wish. Step 3: Gear� Pick the character’s mundane gear. Heroes can begin with anything their players want them to have, provided the GM considers it reasonable. Villains, Foes, and Extras, of course, will have whatever gear the GM thinks they should have. You can find mundane gear in Chapter 6. Step 4: Derived Characteristics� Calculate your Edge, Health, and Resolve. Remember that Foes (and Extras who work like Foes) have half the usual amount of Health, and only Heroes have Resolve. Step 5: Finishing Touches� Create the details and roleplaying elements that make up your finishing touches. These elements are described later in this chapter. As NPCs, Villains, Foes, and Extras have a different set of finishing touches, found in Chapter 9. Step 6: Review� Review your Hero with the GM to make sure your character concept and abilities fit the game. If they don’t, discuss how you can tweak your Hero to resolve any issues. When creating an NPC, the GM should always review them to be sure they haven’t missed anything.

sections.heading: RULE UNO
sections.text: If you want to break this game, you can. This is a superhero game, one that lets you play anything from an ordinary guy with a serious crime grudge and low impulse control to what can only be described as a demigod. Although we’ve done our best to balance everything, P&P offers an almost infinite number of Power combinations and permutations. That’s a lot of ground to cover. As a result, we have Rule Uno: GMs are the final arbiter of what is allowed in their games, and they can restrict or completely disallow any Power or combination of Powers for any reason whatsoever�

sections.heading: POWER LEVEL
sections.text: Because superheroes can range from skilled humans to cosmic entities, every series has a power level set by the GM. A game’s power level determines how many Hero Points you have to create your Hero, and the maximum rank you can have in any Trait (the Trait Cap). The Power Levels table provides starting Hero Points and Trait Caps for the basic power levels. Remember, this only applies to Heroes. The 200 Hero Points listed for Iconic Heroes is a bare minimum for characters of that power level.

sections.heading: POWER LEVELS — POWER LEVEL HERO POINTS TRAIT CAP
sections.text: Street Level 75 8d Low Level 100 10d Standard 125 12d High Level 150 16d Legendary 175 20d Iconic 200+ 24d You spend Hero Points to purchase your Abilities, Talents, Powers, and Perks, as discussed below. Note that Heroes with lower Ability and Power ranks begin play with more Resolve, an essential resource in the game. As a result, you may want to keep your Ability and Power ranks below the game’s Trait Cap to increase your starting Resolve. Resolve is discussed in more detail in Chapter 5. Additionally, while there aren’t many of them, be careful about Powers that can push otherwise legal Traits above the game’s Trait Cap. For example, when using Growth, your Might rank usually increases to match your Growth rank. However, if your Might rank equals or exceeds your Growth rank, your Might rank increases by 1d instead. That isn’t normally a problem, unless your Might is maxed out at the game’s Trait Cap. If you already have the maximum Might rank allowed, then Growth will push you over the edge. Some GMs will allow this; others won’t. Each GM is free to decide whether to allow edge cases like these in their games, so check with yours if this is relevant to you.

sections.heading: ABILITIES, TALENTS AND POWERS
sections.text: All characters have six Abilities: Agility, Intellect, Might, Perception, Toughness, and Willpower. Each costs 1 Hero Point per rank. For example, 3d Agility costs 3 Hero Points. No Ability can have a rank lower than 1d or higher than the game’s Trait Cap. Ordinary people have 2d in every Ability. All characters have twelve Talents: Academics, Charm, Command, Covert, Investigation, Medicine, Professional, Science, Streetwise, Survival, Technology, and Vehicles. Each costs 1 Hero Point per rank. For example, 6d Charm costs 6 Hero Points. No Talent can have a rank lower than 1d or higher than the game’s Trait Cap. Ordinary people have 2d in every Talent. Most characters—and certainly all Heroes—have one or more Powers. Most Powers cost a number of Hero Points per rank. For example, Flight costs 1 Hero Point per rank, so 10d Flight costs 10 Hero Points. Mind Control, on the other hand, costs 2 Hero Points per rank, so 10d Mind Control costs 20 Hero Points. Some Powers cost 1 Hero Point per 2 ranks. For example, Blind costs that much, so 10d Blind costs 5 Hero Points. When buying Powers that cost 1 Hero Point per 2 ranks, you don’t have to take both ranks in the same Power. For example, you can spend 1 Hero Point to buy 1 rank of Evasion and 1 rank of Swimming, two Powers that cost 1 Hero Point per 2 ranks. Some Powers don’t have ranks. Powers like these cost a flat number of Hero Points rather than a number of points per rank. For example, Communications costs 3 Hero Points. There are also Powers that use one of your other Traits as their baseline rank. When you buy one of these baseline rank Powers, add your baseline rank to however many ranks of the Power you purchase to determine your final rank. For example, Evasion uses Agility as its baseline rank. If you have 5d Agility and you buy 6 ranks of Evasion, you end up with 11d Evasion. Remember, even when dealing with Powers like these, no Trait can have a rank higher than the game’s Trait Cap (subject to optional exceptions discussed in Chapter 9).

sections.heading: PACKAGES
sections.text: If you want to expedite character creation and save yourself a few Hero Points as well, you can purchase one of the following packages. These packages provide you starting Ability and Talents ranks at a small discount. The Civilian Package gives you 2d in all Abilities and Talents. The Hero Package gives you 3d in all Abilities and 2d in all Talents. The Superhero Package gives you 3d in all Abilities and Talents. If you buy one of these packages, you can’t lower any of these Traits below these values, but you can raise them as high as you like (subject to the game’s Trait Cap) by spending extra Hero Points.

sections.heading: HERO PACKAGES — PROS AND CONS
sections.text: Abilities, Talents, and Powers can be modified with options called Pros and Cons. Pros are options that make a Trait more effective or powerful, but they cost extra Hero Points. Cons, on the other hand, are options that make a Trait less effective or powerful, so they save you Hero Points. Pros and Cons usually cost or save you a flat number of points, but a few change a Power’s cost per rank. Regardless of Pros and Cons, no Trait can ever cost less than 1 Hero Point (or 1 Hero Point per 2 ranks).

sections.heading: HERO PACKAGES — SOURCES
sections.text: Because Traits can represent so many different things, every Ability, Talent, and Power has a Source that indicates what it’s supposed to be: a natural ability, a learned skill, a superpower, a magic spell, etc. The basic Sources are described on the Sources table. Abilities are usually Innate, and Talents are usually Trained, at least when dealing with ordinary people. When dealing with supers and characters who aren’t human, however, anything goes. For example, a robotic character’s Abilities, Talents, and Powers would probably have a Tech Source.

sections.heading: SOURCES — SOURCE DEFAULT RANK DESCRIPTION
sections.text: Shared by all members Innate Toughness of a race or species Magical, divine, infernal, Magic Willpower or otherworldly in nature Originating from a mental Psychic Willpower or mystical inner source Caused by a unique Super Toughness alteration or mutation Mechanical or Tech Toughness technological in nature Developed through practice, Trained Willpower study, or training As noted earlier, some Powers are all-or-nothing abilities that don’t have a rank. Your character either has these abilities or they don’t. Because these Powers have no rank, they use a default rank in place of their rank when dealing with Powers that affect other Powers (such as Power Absorption and Power Mimicry). A Power’s default rank varies depending on its Source, as shown on the Sources table.

sections.heading: PERKS
sections.text: Most Perks cost a flat number of Hero Points. For example, Contacts cost 1 Hero Point apiece, while Fame costs 3 Hero Points. A few Perks cost a variable number of Hero Points, depending on how much you want to get out of them. For example, every Hero Point you spend on Headquarters grants you 3 Base Points to spend on your base of operations.

sections.heading: FLAWS
sections.text: As a starting Hero, you can select up to 3 Flaws. You must select one immediately, but you can leave the other slots open if you prefer, selecting your additional Flaws as ideas come to you. Although you can have fewer than 3 Flaws, this isn’t recommended. Not only do Flaws make your character more interesting, they’re also one of the easiest ways to earn Resolve. You can spend Hero Points to purchase additional Flaws over time, but you can’t have more than 3 at the start.

sections.heading: FINISHING UP
sections.text: The last part of creating your Hero is just bookkeeping. First, select whatever mundane gear you want to carry around with you. Second, calculate your Edge, Health, and Resolve. Third, complete your finishing touches, the narrative details that turn you into a living, breathing character. And fourth, let the GM review your Hero. Darlene is going to create a Hero to play in Danny’s game. As the GM, Danny informs her that this is going to be a Low Level game. That means Darlene has 100 Hero Points to create her Hero, and the game’s Trait Cap is 10d. Darlene already has an idea for the Hero she wants to play, one inspired by a hard-drinking hot mess of a super-powered detective. Darlene spends 50 Hero Points right off the bat to buy the Superhero Package, giving her 3d in all her Abilities and Traits. She spends 14 more Hero Points on her Abilities: 3 to raise her Agility to 6d, 5 to raise her Might to 8d, 3 to raise her Perception to 6d, and 3 to raise her Toughness to 6d. She also puts 16 more Hero Points into her Talents: 3 to raise her Command to 6d, 3 to raise her Covert to 6d, 7 to raise her Investigation to 10d, and 3 to raise her Streetwise to 6d. Darlene decides that, like most normal people, her Abilities are Innate, and her Talents are Trained. The only exceptions are her Might and Toughness, both of which are Super, the result of a freak accident in her early teens. With only 20 Hero Points left, Darlene spends 16 of them on her Powers: 5 for 8d Armor (Armor has a baseline rank equal to half her 6d Toughness, or 3d, so she only need to buy 5 ranks of Armor for a final rank of 8d), 5 for one point of Determination, and 6 for Regeneration. Darlene decides that like her Might and Toughness, her Armor and Regeneration Powers are also Super. Determination is a special Power that doesn’t have a Source. Darlene spends her last 4 Hero Points on Contacts, giving her well-connected Hero 4 contacts: a journalist, someone in law enforcement, a local politician, and one lowlife criminal. With her characteristics out of the way, Darlene doesn’t waste a moment coming up with her Flaws, which is what she finds most interesting about this character anyway. Scanning the Flaws, she quickly settles on a Compulsion (drinking), a Quirk (being obnoxious and sarcastic), and a Relationship (with her best friend, someone she’s known since high school). At this point, Darlene chooses her mundane gear, which is easy because she only carries her keys, wallet, and phone around with her (assuming she doesn’t forget them at home). She then calculates her Edge, Health, and Resolve and begins to work on her finishing touches. Once she’s done, she’ll review everything with Danny the GM to make sure her Hero will work for the game he has planned.

sections.heading: ABILITIES
sections.text: Abilities represent basic physical and mental characteristics. All characters have six Abilities: Agility, Intellect, Might, Perception, Toughness, and Willpower. The Ability Ranks table provides a rough guideline of the relative power levels of Ability ranks 1d to 6d. Ordinary human beings have Ability ranks in this range, with 2d being the average and 6d being the blurry line between exceptional and superhuman. Of course, since comic books are full of supposedly ordinary people with extraordinary abilities, this is more of a rough guideline than a hard cap for ordinary human characters. Even so, ordinary humans almost never have more than 6d Might or Toughness.

sections.heading: ABILITY RANKS — ABILITY RANK
sections.text: Impaired 1d Undeveloped 2d Developed 3d Noteworthy 4d Exceptional 5d Peak 6d

sections.heading: AGILITY
sections.text: Agility covers coordination, dexterity, nimbleness, reflexes, and speed. It is used to perform acrobatic or athletic activities like balancing, climbing, diving, jumping, and running. Agility also applies when firing mundane ranged weapons and defending against attacks. Last, you can substitute half your Agility for your Covert when making challenge rolls to hide, move quietly, or avoid detection.

sections.heading: INTELLECT
sections.text: Intellect represents your intelligence, knowledge, memory, shrewdness, and overall level of education. Use this Trait to make intelligence-based challenge rolls that don’t fall under any of your Talents. In fact, you can substitute half your Intellect for any Talent when making challenge rolls to determine what you know about something (but not when trying to actually do anything— knowing how to perform a heart transplant, for example, is very different from actually performing one).

sections.heading: MIGHT
sections.text: Might is your sheer physical strength. It is used to perform armed and unarmed close combat attacks and feats of strength like lifting heavy objects or tearing things apart. The Weight table indicates the maximum amount of weight you can lift, depending on your Might. When not referring to Might, the rank that corresponds to an object’s weight on this table is sometimes called its weight rank. Last, Might can also come into play when determining your Health.

sections.heading: WEIGHT — THE BRUTE OPTION
sections.text: Some characters are much stronger than they are skilled in combat. If that describes you, you can apply the Overkill Con to Might. This unique Con lets you buy Might at half price: you pay 1 Hero Point for every 2 ranks of Might. However, whenever an opponent uses an active defense against your close combat attacks (armed or unarmed), their successes are doubled. Additionally, if you select this option, you use only half your Might rather than your full Might when determining your baseline rank for Powers like Martial Arts and Strike.

sections.heading: PERCEPTION
sections.text: Perception covers your sensory acuity, empathy, intuition, and overall level of awareness. It’s used any time you need to detect or discern hidden things, from assailants to clues to intentions. It also indicates how quickly you can detect, process, and react to new information.

sections.heading: TOUGHNESS
sections.text: Toughness combines your constitution, endurance, and physical resilience. It’s used to resist Powers that affect you physically, as well as physical agents or toxins like diseases, drugs, and poisons. Last, Toughness helps determine how much Health you have and how quickly you recover from injuries.

sections.heading: WILLPOWER
sections.text: Willpower represents your courage, determination, and selfdiscipline. It also indicates the power of your spirit or psyche. It’s used to defend against Powers that affect the mind or soul, and to resist negative emotions and impulses. It can also come into play when determining your Health.

sections.heading: TALENTS
sections.text: Talents represent natural aptitudes and skills picked up through experience or training. All characters have twelve Talents: Academics, Charm, Command, Covert, Investigation, Medicine, Professional, Science, Streetwise, Survival, Technology, and Vehicles. Simply possessing these Talents doesn’t mean you have actual training or experience, not unless you have a rank of 3d or better (and maybe not even then). The Talent Ranks table provides a rough guideline of the relative level of experience, knowledge, or proficiency represented by Talent ranks 1d to 6d. Generally speaking, ordinary human beings have Talent ranks within this range, with 2d being the untrained average, 4d being the average for someone with training or experience, and 6d being the blurry line between exceptional and superhuman. As with Abilities, this is more a rough guideline than a hard cap for ordinary human characters.

sections.heading: TALENT RANKS — TALENT RANK
sections.text: Clueless 1d Unskilled 2d Proficient 3d Advanced 4d Expert 5d Master 6d Talents are supposed to be unrealistically broad, covering a huge variety of disciplines and skills. If you want to tamp this down, you can assume that a Talent’s rank also determines the breadth of your expertise. As a general rule, a rank of 1d to 3d means you have everyday knowledge and expertise, a rank of 4d to 6d indicates uncommon knowledge and expertise, and a rank of 7d or higher represents esoteric knowledge and expertise. For example, it’s reasonable to assume you know how to drive a car with a Vehicles rank of 1d to 3d, a helicopter or an airplane with a Vehicles rank of 4d to 6d, and an experimental prototype starfighter with a Vehicles rank of 7d or higher.

sections.heading: ACADEMICS
sections.text: Academics represents knowledge of scholarly subjects like anthropology, archaeology, art, cultures, history, linguistics, philosophy, psychology, and sociology. It also covers esoteric and fantastical topics like dimensional geography, interplanetary news, magic, the occult, mythical beings, creatures, and places, and so on. If you have at least 4d in this Talent, you are highly educated or well-read.

sections.heading: CHARM
sections.text: Charm reflects attractiveness, empathy, social skills, and force of personality. You use this Talent whenever you try to bluff, charm, deceive, negotiate with, persuade, or seduce someone. Acting also falls under Charm, even when you aren’t using it to deceive anyone.

sections.heading: COMMAND
sections.text: Command concerns getting others to do what you want through force of will. Use this Talent whenever you try to command, frighten, intimidate, interrogate, motivate, or order people around. Apart from that, Command also covers establishing and understanding command structures and protocols.

sections.heading: COVERT
sections.text: Covert applies to intrusion, larceny, shadowing, stealth, and surveillance. It’s used whenever you need to hide, move quietly, follow someone, conduct covert surveillance, or otherwise avoid detection. Covert also helps defeat security measures like alarms, cameras, locks, and traps, as well as to palm items, pick pockets, and perform other acts of nimble-fingered larceny.

sections.heading: INVESTIGATION
sections.text: Investigation concerns the ability to conduct investigations, uncover clues, perform research, interrogate witnesses, analyze data, and make deductive or intuitive leaps. If you have at least 4d in this Talent, you are well-versed in police procedures and your investigations may be admissible in court.

sections.heading: MEDICINE
sections.text: Medicine covers academic and clinical knowledge of medicine and psychology. Assuming you have medical supplies on hand, you can treat wounded characters by making a Hard (2) Medicine roll, healing them of 1 point of damage per net success rolled. Raise the difficulty to Daunting (3) when treating yourself. You can only do this once per patient per day (or once per patient per week if using the Gritty Combat Rules in Chapter 4). If you have at least 4d in this Talent, you are probably a trained doctor. Your parents must be very proud.

sections.heading: PROFESSIONAL
sections.text: Professional reflects your knowledge of the professional world and covers topics like business, economics, and finance. While you may also have a basic understanding of more specific professional areas such as accounting, journalism, law, marketing, politics, or public relations, the Expertise Power represents in-depth knowledge of a specific professional career.

sections.heading: SCIENCE
sections.text: Science covers your knowledge of scientific topics including disciplines like astronomy, biology, botany, chemistry, ecology, genetics, geology, metallurgy, oceanography, physics, and quantum mechanics. It also covers esoteric or fantastical science like paranormal biology or the unique laws of physics in Dimension X! If you have at least 4d in this Talent, you are probably a trained scientist.

sections.heading: STREETWISE
sections.text: Streetwise represents your knowledge of important locations, personalities, and happenings in the criminal underworld, as well as your ability to interact with them. If you have at least 4d in this Talent, your parents probably aren’t nearly as proud as they would have been if you’d gone to med school.

sections.heading: SURVIVAL
sections.text: Survival concerns your ability to survive in the wild. It’s used when building fires, finding food and water, securing shelter, setting traps and snares, tracking, and so on. It also covers practical information about plants and animals found in the wild. Last, this Talent applies when handling animals or riding mounts. If you have at least 4d in this Talent, you may also know how to care for, tame, and train animals.

sections.heading: TECHNOLOGY
sections.text: Technology deals with the creation, modification, and repair of mechanical and technological devices of every kind. This includes computers, electronics, machines, robots, steampunk technology, vehicles, weapons, and anything else you can think of. It also covers the use (and misuse) of high-tech systems like computers and computer networks, as well as equipment like communications and sensor systems. Assuming you have the right tools, you can repair damaged objects by making a Hard (2) Technology roll, repairing 1 point of damage per net success rolled. You can only do this once per object per day.

sections.heading: VEHICLES
sections.text: Vehicles covers the ability to operate all sorts of vehicles. It applies not only to piloting, but also to gunnery, navigation, operations, and even basic maintenance. As mentioned earlier, it might be reasonable to assume you can only drive ordinary vehicles like cars and motorcycles unless you have at least 4d in this Talent, but the GM always has the final say on this.

sections.heading: POWERS
sections.text: Powers are unique special abilities. Some are rather generic, while others are quite specific. This is by design. The generic Powers are there to let you create any ability you can imagine. The specific ones are there so you don’t have to jump through hoops to create an iconic superpower that everyone recognizes. Whether generic or specific, each Power’s entry includes its range, rank, cost, and description. Many also include specific Pros and Cons applicable only to that Power. Range: Powers have a range of Self, Touch, Ranged, Zone, or Special. Self means the Power affects you. Touch means the Power affects beings and/or objects you touch, so they have to be adjacent to you or at least within Close Range so you can move up to them. Ranged means the Power affects beings and/ or objects within Distant Range. Zone is the only range option that incorporates an area of effect, and means the Power always affects everyone and/or everything within 5 to 25 feet of you— you decide how far to extend the Zone each time you use the Power. Last, a few Powers with a range of Special work in some unique way discussed in their descriptions. Rank: This indicates whether the Power has a rank. Power Rank means it does. Baseline Rank (X) also means the Power has a rank, but in this case, the Trait used to determine the Power’s baseline rank is noted in parentheses. When you buy a Power with a baseline rank, add the baseline rank to the number of ranks you purchase to determine the Power’s final rank. Default Rank means the power doesn’t have a rank. You use your Toughness or Willpower (it varies by Source) in place of the Power’s rank when dealing with Powers that affect other Powers. Last, a few Powers with a rank of Special work in some unique way discussed in their descriptions.

sections.heading: SUPER TIP!
sections.text: Remember that the best superhero stories aren’t about having superpowers. They’re about doing the right thing, especially when that thing is dangerous, hard, scary, or requires sacrifice. Don’t let all these superpowers distract you; your games should be about people who are also superheroes rather than about superheroes who are also people. Psychometry Quick Change Radar Regeneration Resistance Running Separation Shockwave Shrinking Slay Slick Speak with Dead Specialty Spinning Star Gate Stretching Strike Stun Summoning Super Senses Super Speed Swimming Swing Line Telekinesis Telepathy Teleportation Time Stop Time Travel Total Recall Tracer Transformation Transmutation Tunneling Two-Dimensional Two-Fisted Vanish Variant Ventriloquism Wall-Crawling Weakness Detection A Power’s rank is normally used to make challenge rolls. It also helps determine what or how much you can do with a Power. For example, Powers that can move physical objects can usually affect up to the amount you could lift with a Might equal to your Power rank. Unless a Power’s description says otherwise, don’t apply its rank to anything other than what the Power does. For example, neither Flight nor Teleportation specify that your Power rank determines how much you can carry while using those Powers, so that amount is determined as usual (i.e., by your Might). If you have a Power that lets you move faster than normal or in ways an ordinary person can’t (a Travel Power), your Power rank usually indicates your maximum speed, as shown on the Speed table. Ordinary people move at 3d speed, sound travels at 9d, and light clocks in at a brisk 27d. The rank that corresponds to an object’s speed on this table is sometimes called its speed rank.

No Power can ever cost less than 1 Hero Point (or 1 Hero Point per 2 ranks) regardless of its Cons. A few Powers with a cost of Special work in some unique way discussed in their descriptions. Description: This describes what the Power does and how it works. If a Power can be used to attack or affect other characters, its description indicates the Traits that may be used to resist such efforts. The defender always uses whichever Trait offers them the best chance of success when making challenge rolls to resist a Power. Occasionally, a Power’s description may also include notes concerning its use and suggestions to the GM regarding what effect it may have on the game.

sections.heading: ADAPTATION
sections.text: Self • Default Rank • 12 Hero Points Your body instantly adapts to your surroundings, letting you breathe, move around, sense things, and survive in alien or hostile environments. For example, you might grow gills, fins, and a membrane over your eyes while underwater, plus you’d become immune to undersea pressure and temperature.

sections.heading: ALTERNATE FORM
sections.text: Self • Default Rank • 4 Hero Points per power level You can turn into a different form. Create this form as a separate Hero (see below). Your alternate form can be of any power level up to but not higher than yours. For example, if you are a Standard Hero, your other form can be Street Level, Low Level, or Standard. This Power’s cost varies depending on your other form’s power level, as indicated on the Alternate Form table. Your other form’s power level only affects the number of Hero Points you have to create it, not its Trait Cap. Both forms must pay for this Power. As you gain extra Hero Points, you can spend them differently for each form. Buy this Power multiple times if you want multiple forms, but each form must pay this Power’s total cost. For example, if you buy this Power twice to gain 2 alternate Standard forms, all three forms will have to pay the 24 Hero Points. When creating alternate forms, you must give them their own their Abilities, Talents, and Powers, although some of these Traits may share the same rank across multiple forms. Your various forms may share Perks and Flaws, or they might have their own. This varies by character. No matter how many forms you can assume, you only have one pool of Resolve: use the lowest Resolve among your various forms as your actual Resolve. For example, if you have two forms, one that would have 6 Resolve as a separate character and one that would have 1 Resolve as a separate character, you have 1 Resolve.

sections.heading: ALTERNATE FORM — POWER LEVEL COST
sections.text: Street Level 4 Low Level 8 Standard 12 High Level 16 Legendary 20 Iconic 24 CON Independent Forms (−1 per power level): Each of your forms has a separate identity, memory, and personality, and your various forms may or may not get along very well.

sections.heading: ANIMAL CONTROL
sections.text: Ranged • Power Rank • 1 Hero Point per rank Whether through mind control or friendly communication, you can make animals do what you want for the Power’s duration by making an Animal Control roll against their Willpower. PRO Calling (+2): You can call out to distant animals, which lets you use this Power on creatures within Extreme Range (basically as far as your call can be heard). Controlled animals race to your location, and the Power’s duration doesn’t begin to run until they arrive. CON Only X (−2 or −4): You can only control a specific category, group, or type of animal specified when you buy this Power. This is normally a −2 Con, but if the group of animals is very narrow or of limited utility (such as aquatic animals), this becomes a −4 Con instead.

sections.heading: ANIMAL EMPATHY
sections.text: Self • Default Rank • 1 Hero Point You share an empathic understanding with animals. Animals are unlikely to attack you without good reason, such as if they’re injured or protecting their young, and even then, you may be able to dissuade them (especially if you have snacks because, well, because snacks). PRO Speech (+2): You can communicate with animals. GMs determine how intelligent mundane animals are in their games and how they react to this. One could reasonably assume that domesticated animals and those comfortable with humans are usually friendly unless trained to be otherwise, but wild animals are likely much more cautious.

sections.heading: ANIMAL MIMICRY
sections.text: Self • Power Rank • 2 Hero Points per rank You can mimic animals, gaining their Powers at the lower of their Power rank or your Power rank. When mimicking an animal, you gain all their Powers, even ones that would seem to rely on body parts you lack (claws, gills, wings, etc.). You also gain the animal’s Agility, Might, Perception, and Toughness at the lesser of their respective Ability ranks or your Power rank, but only if their Ability ranks exceed yours. If any of your Abilities are greater, they aren’t affected. You can mimic any natural animal you are familiar with, whether alive or extinct. As for magical creatures like dragons and unicorns, that’s up to the GM. If you are an alien, you mimic alien animals. For the sake of game balance (and everyone’s sanity), these alien animals look different but have the same characteristics as the Earth animals described in Chapter 8. Mimicking an animal or changing your selection is a free action, but you can only do so once per page, twice if you forego your next turn to act. PRO Enhanced (+4): Whenever you mimic an animal, you can use your Power rank in place of its highest ranked Trait. You can do this for only one Trait per animal (pick one if several Traits have the same rank). For example, gorillas have 6d Might and Toughness. If you use 10d Animal Mimicry to mimic a gorilla, you can give yourself 10d in one of those Abilities. PRO Selection (+4): You can mimic more than one animal at a time, using the best Traits from among all the animals you are mimicking, but this lowers your effective Power rank by 1d per extra animal being mimicked at the same time.

sections.heading: ANIMATION
sections.text: Ranged • Power Rank • 2 Hero Points per rank You can animate images and objects, bringing them to life until the end of the scene or until you dismiss them. Animated images step off the page, screen, wall, or surface on which you found them and grow to their actual real-world size. Animated objects, meanwhile, begin moving in whatever way seems most natural: statues twist and bend as if their joints were real, flexible objects move like snakes, solid objects gain a cartoonish level of flexibility that allows them to move around, weapons leap into the air as if wielded by invisible enemies, and so on. Animated beings have three Abilities, Agility, Might, and Toughness, plus whatever Powers they should reasonably possess. For example, an animated image of a winged dragon should probably have Blast (Fire) and Flight (whether or not the image was breathing fire or flying), while an animated marble statue should probably have Solid Form. One of your creation’s Traits shares this Power’s rank; the rest have a rank equal to half your Animation rank. You determine which Trait uses your full Power rank on a case-by-case basis. Animated beings are inanimate objects that lack mental faculties and act only in response to your mental commands. You can animate more than one thing at a time, but this lowers your effective Animation rank by 1d per extra object. You can’t animate a physical object whose Structure exceeds your Power rank.

sections.heading: ARMOR
sections.text: Self • Baseline Rank (½ Toughness) • 1 Hero Point per rank You have armor or a personal force field that repels damage. You can use this Power as a passive defense against physical attacks and energy attacks, regardless of the type of damage they inflict. You are completely immune to such attacks if their attack rank is less than or equal to half your Armor rank (unless they have the Penetrating Pro). When dealing with Minions, use their unmodified Threat rank as their attack rank when determining if you are immune to their attacks. CON Activated (−1): This Power represents a defense you must activate, like a personal force shield or body coating. Although you can do this as a free action, the Power stops working if you are knocked out or otherwise rendered unconscious. CON Reactive (−2): This Power represents something like bracers or a shield that you use to block or deflect incoming attacks. Accordingly, it’s considered an active defense.

sections.heading: ASTRAL PROJECTION
sections.text: Self • Default Rank • 12 Hero Points Your astral form can leave your physical body. You gain Invisible, Phasing (Intangible), and Super Senses (Astral Sight) while in astral form, although you can make yourself visible if you wish. You can also fly in this form, as if you had Flight at your Willpower rank. As long as you are using this Power, your physical body lies dormant, although you will know instantly if it gets moved or harmed.

sections.heading: ATTUNED
sections.text: Self • Default Rank • 3 Hero Points You are attuned to some aspect of nature like currents and tides, plate tectonics, or weather patterns, to a particular geographic area like a city, forest, jungle, or sacred grove, or to the larger cosmos in general. You can tell when dramatic or unusual disturbances or phenomenon are imminent within your area of attunement. If attuned to a geographic area, you can also tell when powerful beings enter or leave, possibly even when they’re born and when they die, depending on how powerful they are. Your level of sensitivity varies depending on the scope of your attunement. For example, a magician attuned to the mansion that serves as her sanctum sanctorum is keenly aware of everything that happens in her home, while a cosmically attuned galactic guardian is only sensitive to cosmic beings, events, and forces. This Power automatically provides you with basic information, but you can spend 1 Resolve to ask the GM for more in-depth information, assuming there’s any to be had. The information you receive may sometimes be incomplete or misleading, but it is always truthful.

sections.heading: AURA
sections.text: Self • Power Rank • 2 Hero Points per rank Your body inflicts a specific type of energy damage on contact (pick one). Anyone who touches you suffers an attack using your Aura rank that can only be resisted with passive defenses. This also applies to anyone who strikes you in unarmed combat (if you resist an unarmed attack with a passive defense, assume the attacker strikes you, even if you suffer no damage). You can also use Aura to perform close combat attacks that inflict energy damage. If you already have a close combat attack at an equal or greater rank, use its rank +1d instead. Physical objects tend to burn, dissolve, or melt near you, so you suffer no damage from mundane physical objects with a Structure lower than your Aura rank. Wooden weapons usually have 6d Structure, while bullets and metal weapons usually have 9d Structure. CON Spines (−2): Your body has a covering of quills or spines that inflict physical damage rather than energy damage. As a result, this Power provides no protection against physical attacks.

sections.heading: BANISH
sections.text: Ranged • Power Rank • 1 Hero Point per rank You can banish a target to another time, place, or dimension (pick one) by making a Banish roll against their Willpower or one of their active defenses. If you wish, you can specify that your version of the Power is resisted with Toughness instead of Willpower, but active defenses always apply as well. You can’t send targets anywhere that would be harmful or from which they can’t return, but characters run by an evil GM have no such restrictions, and all GMs are evil. Even though a banished target isn’t actually present, you can keep using this Power on them until they’ve been defeated—in this case, you aren’t so much attacking as concentrating on keeping them away—but the effect is the same. When Heroes get banished, they often wind up in dangerous or at least interesting locales. Banished Heroes still get their actions, which they can use to fight off hungry monsters, explore strange alien vistas, or do whatever else is appropriate for the place in which they find themselves.

sections.heading: BLAST
sections.text: Ranged • Power Rank • 1 Hero Point per rank You can fire a damaging ranged attack. You must specify the kind of damage inflicted when you buy this Power (unless you apply the Weapons Con discussed below). PRO Block (+2): You can use the Power as an active defense against ranged physical and energy attacks (but not against area attacks) by shooting them down. If you forego your next action, this turns the attack into a blast duel, a 3-exchange contest, with each character using their Blast Power against the other. The first exchange happens immediately. The second happens on your next turn to act. The third and final exchange happens on your opponent’s next turn to act. Whoever wins the contest hits their opponent with a number of successes equal to their Blast rank, and this attack can only be resisted with passive defenses. PRO Melee (+2): You can use the Power as an active defense against close combat attacks. The Power may look different when used in this fashion. For example, your fire Blast might take on the appearance of a flaming sword whenever you get into close combat. CON Subdual (−1): The Power inflicts subdual damage. CON Weapons (−1): This Power represents mastery of a group of weapons as broad or narrow as you like— the level of specificity doesn’t matter. You have to be armed with that type of weapon to use the Power. This lets you use your Blast rank (instead of your Ability plus Weapon Bonus) to make attack rolls while so armed. Otherwise, the weapon works as usual and deals whatever type of damage it normally inflicts.

sections.heading: BLENDING
sections.text: Self • Default Rank • 3 Hero Points Your coloring can change to match your environment, granting you a +3d bonus on Covert rolls to avoid being seen. If you remain still, you can also make a Covert roll at half your rank (after taking the +3d bonus into account) to avoid being seen when you would otherwise be in plain view.

sections.heading: BLIND
sections.text: Ranged • Power Rank • 1 Hero Point per 2 ranks You can blind a living target for the Power’s duration by making a Blind roll against their Toughness or one of their active defenses. Targets affected by this Power suffer a −3d penalty to their attack and active defense rolls in combat unless they have a Power like Blind Fighting or Radar that compensates for this. You can have a version of Blind that affects a sense other than vision, but you and the GM will have to determine whether this has any mechanical effect in combat.

sections.heading: BLIND FIGHTING
sections.text: Self • Default Rank • 3 Hero Points You don’t rely on vision in combat. As a result, you suffer no penalties or adverse effects when fighting in the dark or against opponents you can’t see, whatever the reason.

sections.heading: BLINK
sections.text: Self • Power Rank • 1 Hero Point per rank You use your Powers to blink in and out of reality during combat. This can mean any number of things: phasing in and out of the physical world, rapidly changing your size and/or shape, sliding through dimensional portals, teleporting around opponents, or anything else you can image. Use Blink instead of Might when making close combat attack rolls and instead of Agility when making active defense rolls and movement rolls (although this isn’t a Travel Power and doesn’t actually let you move any faster than normal). If you have these Traits or other applicable Powers (such as Evasion, Martial Arts, or Strike) at an equal or greater rank, use their ranks +1d instead.

sections.heading: BOOST
sections.text: Self • Baseline Rank (Special) • Special You can raise the rank of one specific Ability, Talent, or Power (pick one) up to this Power’s rank. This Power costs as many Hero Points per rank as the Trait it affects and uses that Trait as its baseline rank. Cons must be applied to this Power to indicate how and when it operates; otherwise it’s meaningless. CON Rage (−2): The Power activates when you get really mad. However, your Intellect and all your Talents drop to 1d as long as you remain angry enough to use this Power. Your rage always subsides by the end of a scene. You should also consider the Quirk (Bad Temper) Flaw.

sections.heading: BUFF
sections.text: Zone • Default Rank • 12 Hero Points You can spend 1 point of Resolve to bolster yourself and all allies within range, granting you all a +1d bonus on all challenge rolls for the rest of the scene. Your allies must remain within the Power’s area of effect to get this bonus. You must use an action to activate this Power, but once you do, you can sustain it as a free action. This Power always expires at the end of a scene, if not sooner. Buff can’t be stacked, not even if multiple characters have it from different Sources. PRO Greater (6): You can increase the bonus provided by this Power by +1d per extra point of Resolve spent, up to a maximum of 3 points of Resolve for a +3d bonus. Certain NPCs may be able to push this envelope, but that’s within the GM’s purview.

sections.heading: CLAIRVOYANCE
sections.text: Self • Default Rank • 9 Hero Points You can see things at distant locations as if you were there. If the location is somehow shielded from you, you must make a Willpower roll against the shielding rank to use this Power. Clairvoyance works at any distance. You can even peer into other dimensions by making a Superhuman (6) Willpower roll. Although you normally observe locations, you can instead focus on a specific person or object. To do this, you must be familiar with the subject or have some meaningful item or fetish that connects you. This won’t tell you where that subject is located unless something you see gives that away.

sections.heading: CLOUD MINDS
sections.text: Ranged • Power Rank • 1 Hero Point per rank You can cloud the minds of living beings, effectively making yourself invisible to everyone within Distant Range. Characters affected by this Power can’t see, hear, or otherwise detect you in any way unless they make a successful Willpower roll against your Cloud Minds. Characters cannot attempt to resist this Power unless you move within Close Range of them or take some action that would make your presence evident. You must spend 1 action per page to maintain this Power.

sections.heading: COMMUNICATIONS
sections.text: Self • Default Rank • 3 Hero Points You can detect, receive, store, and transmit communications and information across whatever networks exist in your game. Your range is worldwide or farther if it makes sense in the game world. Although you can interface with mundane communication systems, you don’t require physical infrastructure like cell towers or communication satellites. This Power works automatically, but you may have to make Technology rolls to do things like tap into secure networks or channels.

sections.heading: CONSTRUCTS
sections.text: Ranged • Power Rank • 3 Hero Points per rank You can create and manipulate constructs of solid force. You can create simple geometric shapes and physical objects like airfoils, balls, bars, cages, columns, crowbars, hammers, hands, nets, parachutes, ramps, ropes, walls, wedges, and so on. Your constructs have a Structure equal to your Power rank and can be as rigid or as flexible as you like. You can use them to grab, lift, or exert force with an effective Might equal to your Constructs rank. You have complete control over your constructs, and can alter their size, shape, and rigidity as desired. You can use this Power to attack targets in any number of ways such as by creating constructs in the air above them and letting them drop, flinging them at your targets like projectiles, and so on. You can also defend yourself against physical and energy attacks by creating momentary shields and walls. Your constructs last for the rest of the scene, until you dispel them, or until they’re destroyed. You can create and control multiple constructs at one time, but this lowers your effective rank by 1d per extra construct and you still suffer the usual multiple action penalties if you perform more than one action per page. PRO Devices (+2 per rank): You can create complex machines and intricate shapes that can imitate other Powers. This works like a broad version of Omni-Power.

sections.heading: DANGER SENSE
sections.text: Self • Baseline Rank (Perception) • 1 Hero Point per rank You have the uncanny ability to detect immediate physical danger, even from sources you have no way of sensing, like a bomb under the floor. Use this Power instead of Perception when making rolls to detect danger and when determining your Edge. Additionally, you can make active defense rolls even when caught by surprise, using the lesser of your active defense rank or your Danger Sense rank.

sections.heading: DARKNESS
sections.text: Zone • Default Rank • 6 Hero Points You can fill the space around you with darkness, dust, fog, smoke, or some other obscuring element through which only you and those unaffected by the obscuring element can see. Make up the specifics when you select this Power. For example, Super Senses (Night Vision or Thermal Vision) might let you see through darkness, while Super Senses (Thermal Vision or Ultra Vision) might let you see through fog or smoke. Targets affected by this Power suffer a −3d penalty to their attack and active defense rolls in combat unless they have a Power like Blind Fighting or Radar that compensates for this.

sections.heading: DAZZLE
sections.text: Zone • Power Rank • 1 Hero Point per rank You can emit a blinding flash that overwhelms the senses of all living beings within range, friend and foe alike, by making a Dazzle roll against their Willpower or one of their active defenses. Targets affected by this Power are stunned for one page (until after your next turn to act) and then blinded for whatever’s left of the Power’s duration. Stunned targets cannot move or perform actions. Blinded targets are affected as per Blind. Unlike most Powers, you can’t use this on a target already suffering from its effects, so you can’t stack the duration by attacking the same target multiple times. CON Deafen (−1): The Power leaves targets deafened rather than blinded after the stun effect wears off. Although preferable to being blinded, deafened characters are disoriented and suffer a −1d penalty on all challenge rolls for the rest of the Power’s duration. The GM will have to decide if characters with Powers like Blind Fighting or Radar can ignore this penalty.

sections.heading: DEFLECTION
sections.text: Self • Power Rank • 1 Hero Point per rank You can deflect and redirect ranged attacks (but not area attacks). Decide whether you can deflect physical attacks or energy attacks when you select this Power. You can use your Deflection rank as an active defense against that type of attack. Whenever such an attack fails to harm you, you can spend a free action to immediately redirect it using the lesser of the attack’s rank or your Deflection rank to make your attack roll. You can deflect any number of attacks without penalty, but you suffer a cumulative −2d penalty on your rolls to redirect these attacks if you try to redirect two or more on the same page. If you wish, you can double the cost of this Power and spend 2 Hero Points per rank to be able to deflect both physical attacks and energy attacks. CON Only X (−4): You can only deflect one specific type of object or energy (pick one).

sections.heading: DENSITY
sections.text: Self • Power Rank • 1 Hero Point per rank You can increase your density. While dense, you can substitute your current Density rank for your Might and Toughness, and you gain Armor at that rank as well. If you already have any of these Traits at an equal or greater rank, use their ranks +1d instead. You also become heavier when using this Power: at rank 3d or higher, your weight rank equals your current Density rank. Most ordinary floors will have trouble supporting your weight much past 6d Density.

sections.heading: DETECTION
sections.text: Ranged • Power Rank • 1 Hero Point per 2 ranks You can detect the presence and pinpoint the location of something: a particular type of energy or matter, a certain kind of being or object, a specific emotion or mental state, life, death, taxes, or whatever else you want. This Power normally works automatically, but you may have to make challenge rolls using your Power rank to detect things that are faint, hidden, or otherwise hard to notice. Unlike most ranged Powers, Detection works out to Extreme Range. PRO Long Range (+1): The Power works at incredible and possibly interplanetary distances. In effect, it extends as far as the Heroes need, out to the very limits of Plot Device Range.

sections.heading: DETERMINATION
sections.text: Self • Special • 5 Hero Points per 1 Resolve Your determination is legendary, even for a Hero. You begin every issue with 1 extra point of Resolve for every 5 Hero Points you put into Determination. This Power has no rank and can’t be absorbed, drained, mimicked, or affected by other abilities. Only Heroes can make use of this power.

sections.heading: DIMENSIONAL TRAVEL
sections.text: Self • Default Rank • 6 Hero Points You can travel to other dimensions. Although it involves travel, you must spend an action to use this Power. The first time you travel to an unfamiliar dimension, you arrive at a random location determined by the GM. After that, you return to where you were when you left, or you can spend 1 Resolve to arrive at another familiar location of your choosing. You can use this Power a number of times per issue equal to your Willpower without paying anything. Each use after that costs 1 Resolve. PRO Portal (+2): You can create portals through which others can travel.

sections.heading: DISPEL
sections.text: Ranged • Power Rank • 1 Hero Point per 2 ranks You can free a being or object within range from the effect of any Power that has an ongoing duration by making a Dispel roll against that Power’s rank. You can only dispel Powers from one Source (pick one). This doesn’t prevent a Power from working; it merely ends the Power’s duration. However, you can use Dispel as an active defense against Powers that inflict special effects. PRO Also X (Special): You can dispel Powers from more than one Source. Every additional Source increases this Power’s cost by 1 Hero Point per 2 ranks. For example, this Power costs 1 Hero Point per rank if you can dispel Magic and Psychic Powers.

sections.heading: DRAIN
sections.text: Ranged • Power Rank • 1 Hero Point per 2 ranks You can drain a character’s Abilities, Talents, and Powers from a specific Source (pick one) by making a Drain roll against their highest-ranked Trait that shares this Source. Drained Abilities and Talents drop to 1d for the Power’s duration, while drained Powers completely stop working. Abilities, Talents, and Powers from other Sources are unaffected and can’t be used to resist this Power. PRO Also X (Special): You can affect Traits from more than one Source. Every additional Source increases this Power’s cost by 1 Hero Point per 2 ranks. For example, this Power costs 3 Hero Points per 2 ranks if you can affect Innate, Super, and Trained Traits. CON Only X (−2 or −4): You can only affect one type of Trait. This is usually a −2 Con and means you can only affect Abilities, Talents, or Powers (pick one). If you can only affect one specific Ability, Talent, or Power (again, pick one), this is a −4 Con instead.

sections.heading: DUPLICATION
sections.text: Self • Default Rank • 25 Hero Points You can spend an action to create a duplicate of yourself. Your duplicate is an exact copy of you but lacks this Power. This doesn’t grant you extra uses of Powers with limited uses like Dimensional Travel or Healing. Although you can both use these Powers, each use is tallied against their limit. Your duplicate lacks Resolve, but you can spend yours on their behalf. Your duplicate vanishes when either of you is defeated. Once they vanish, a duplicate can’t be summoned again in the same scene. You can buy this Power multiple times if you want to be able to create multiple duplicates. Because this Power effectively gives you an extra character to control, GMs should feel free to limit or prohibit its use.

sections.heading: ELEMENTAL CONTROL
sections.text: Ranged • Power Rank • 3 Hero Points per rank You can create and control one type of energy, matter, or phenomenon (called an element). Common elements include air, cold, earth and stone, electricity, fire, friction, garbage, gravity, heat, ice, light, magnetism, metal, plants, plasma, radiation, sand, sound, vibrations, water, weather, and wood. By manipulating this element, you can create effects that imitate other Powers at this Power’s rank, provided what you are doing makes comic book sense. In effect, this Power works like Constructs and/or a narrow version of Omni-Power, depending on what you can control. PRO Matter Creation (+1 per rank): Matter created with this power is normally unstable, dissolving or dissipating by the end of the scene (as per Constructs). However, you can create stable matter that will last as long as ordinary matter of its type by spending an amount of Resolve equal to the weight rank of the stable matter you wish to create (minimum 1 point). You must be able to control a type of matter to select this Pro. CON Only Control (−1 per rank): You can control the element, but you can’t create it. Instead, you must rely on whatever is available within range.

sections.heading: EMOTION CONTROL
sections.text: Ranged • Power Rank • 1 Hero Point per rank You can cause anyone within range to experience an overwhelming emotion or mental state such as anger, confusion, fear, love, lust, or sadness by making an Emotion Control roll against their Willpower. The GM determines how the target reacts based on the circumstances and the feeling generated, but the emotion can run from mild to overwhelming and the reaction is often powerful and irrational. CON Only X (−2): You can only generate one emotion or mental state (pick one). CON Pheromones (−2): Your Power is chemical in nature. Characters use the greater of their Toughness or Willpower to resist it. Additionally, characters who don’t breathe are immune to this Power, as are those protected by life support systems or immune to toxins.

sections.heading: ENERGY ABSORPTION
sections.text: Self • Power Rank • 1 or 3 Hero Points per rank You can absorb one type of energy (pick one) by siphoning it from a nearby source or getting struck by an attack. You absorb a number of ranks equal to the lesser of the energy’s rank or your Power rank. You are immune to energy attacks with a rank less than or equal to your Power rank, and you can use this Power as a passive defense against energy attacks with a greater rank. Absorbed energy must be spent immediately in one of the following ways. It can boost your Agility, Might, or Toughness to the rank of the absorbed energy until the end of the following page. It can grant you a +1d bonus to all rolls until the end of the following page. It can be fired out as a Blast at the rank of the absorbed energy. Or it can heal one point of damage for every 2 full ranks absorbed. Energy Absorption costs 1 Hero Point per rank unless you can absorb kinetic energy (i.e., all physical attacks), in which case it costs 3 Hero Points per rank and is subject to the GM’s approval. PRO Also X (+2): You can absorb one extra type of energy (other than kinetic energy) each time you select this Pro. This Pro cannot be used to add kinetic energy to this Power after the fact.

sections.heading: SUPER TIP!
sections.text: P&P is not a granular, skill-based game, but you can use Expertise to much the same effect by ruling that characters must have an appropriate Expertise in certain instances.

sections.heading: ENSNARE
sections.text: Ranged • Power Rank • 1 Hero Point per rank You can ensnare an opponent in something like ice, vines, or webbing that prevents them from taking physical actions for the Power’s duration by making an Ensnare roll against their Might or one of their active defenses. Targets can also use Aura as a passive defense against this attack. PRO Line (+2): This power involves some sort of line or tether that lets you pull an ensnared target to you as long as their weight rank doesn’t exceed your Ensnare rank. If your target weighs more than you can lift, however, you may be the one moving. CON Immobilize (−2): You only glue targets to one spot. Targets can’t move from their current location, but they remain free to take whatever other physical actions they wish.

sections.heading: EVASION
sections.text: Self • Baseline Rank (Agility) • 1 Hero Point per 2 ranks You are a nimble combatant who’s always in motion. You can use Evasion instead of Agility when making active defense rolls and movement rolls (although this isn’t a Travel Power and doesn’t actually let you move any faster than normal). You can also use Evasion in place of Agility when performing or resisting combat stunts.

sections.heading: EXPERTISE
sections.text: Self • Baseline Rank (Special) • 1 Hero Point per 2 ranks You have a specialization of some kind, often a specific area of knowledge, proficiency, or skill. Your specialization must fall under one of your Abilities or Talents. Make up the specialization and specify which Trait it falls under when you select this Power. For example, you could have Expertise (Agility: Firearms) or Expertise (Technology: Robotics). The same specialization may fall under more than one Trait (for example, a military science specialty could reasonably fall under Academics or Professional). Use this Power’s rank in place of the Trait your Expertise falls under whenever your specialization applies. This Power’s baseline rank equals the rank of the Ability or Talent it falls under.

sections.heading: EXTRA LIMBS
sections.text: Self • Default Rank • 3 Hero Points You have extra arms, prehensile hair, a prehensile tail, tentacles, or something similar. Aside from the numerous advantages of having extra manipulative limbs, you gain a +2d bonus to your attack and defense rolls when grappling. The GM may also let you apply this bonus to other actions that could reasonably benefit from having extra limbs, such as climbing and swimming.

sections.heading: FLIGHT
sections.text: Self • Power Rank • 1 Hero Point per rank This Travel Power lets you fly like a bird, or a plane, or a cow with jet engines strapped onto its terrified back. You get the idea. Flight requires more room to maneuver than most Travel Powers, so you must halve your effective Flight rank indoors unless you are operating in an exceptionally large space. PRO Spaceflight (+2): You can move faster than light in outer space, allowing you to cross interstellar distances, assuming you can survive out there. CON Gliding (−2): You glide rather than fly, so you must descend at least one story (about 15 feet) per page unless you can catch a rising current of air. CON Levitation (−4): You can only move up and down or hover in place. CON Slides (−2): You surf on slides of matter or energy that you create as you travel, so you have to stay within Distant Range of the ground, buildings, or other large solid objects. CON Wings (−2): You need room to spread your wings, so you can’t fly in cramped spaces (including most indoor locations), thin atmospheres, or the vacuum of space.

sections.heading: FORCE FIELD
sections.text: Self • Power Rank • 1 Hero Point per rank You can project a force field that repels damage. Characters protected by the force field can use your Power rank as a passive defense against both physical attacks and energy attacks, and are completely immune to such attacks if their attack rank is less than or equal to half your Force Field rank. When dealing with Minions, use their unmodified Threat rank as their attack rank when determining if protected characters are immune to their attacks. This Power blocks physical objects and energy attacks. It does not affect ambient energy that isn’t intense enough to inflict harm (ordinary sounds, room temperate, visible light, etc.), nor does it block indirect Power effects. For example, someone with Darkness could affect the environment across a force field. This Power does not affect mental attacks in any way. You can shape your force field however you wish, anything from a flat plane to a bubble that protects you and everyone adjacent to you. Apply the Zone Pro to shield large areas, the Ranged Pro to shield things at a distance, or the Area Pro to shield large areas at a distance. You must spend an action to activate this Power, but you can then maintain it as a free action. You can maintain multiple force fields at the same time, but this lowers your effective Power rank by 1d per extra force field. PRO Inviolate (+1 per rank): Whenever you raise a force field, you can spend 1 Resolve to have the field repel not only direct attacks, but also all Power effects of equal or lesser rank. An inviolate force field can even be used as a passive defense against mental attacks. PRO Permeable (+6): If you wish, you can allow attacks to pass unhindered through the force field in one direction, letting you and your allies attack normally while protected by the field. An inviolate force field (as described above) can’t also be permeable. CON Collapsible (−2): Your force field collapses when struck by an attack whose rank exceeds your Power rank. Although the Power still acts as a passive defense against that attack, you will have to spend an action if you wish to reactivate your force field. CON Ward (−1): Your Power protects against mental attacks and effects rather than physical ones. This is the only kind of force field that can hold a character using Phasing (Intangible).

sections.heading: FORM
sections.text: This Power lets you turn yourself into something other than flesh and blood. The details vary depending on what you can turn yourself into.

sections.heading: ENERGY FORM
sections.text: Self • Power Rank • 3 Hero Points per rank You can turn into one type of energy (pick one), gaining Aura and Flight at this Power’s rank. In this form, you are weightless and immune to physical and energy attacks and effects. While you can’t carry or touch anything, you aren’t truly intangible: objects and force fields can contain you. You also become vulnerable to things that can affect the energy that forms your body. For example, if you are composed of electricity, things that can absorb electricity may be able to harm you. PRO Also X (+2): You can turn into one additional type of energy for every 2 extra Hero Points.

sections.heading: GASEOUS FORM
sections.text: Self • Default Rank • 6 Hero Points You can turn into a gas, gaining 1d Flight. In this form you are weightless and immune to physical attacks and effects (including energy attacks), and you can move through any opening through which gases can pass. You can’t carry, touch, or affect anything physical while in this form, but you become vulnerable to things that can affect gases.

sections.heading: LIQUID FORM
sections.text: Self • Default Rank • 12 Hero Points You can turn into a liquid or a collection of fine particles like dust or sand, making you immune to physical attacks (but not energy attacks) and letting you pass through any opening liquids can pass through. You can nevertheless solidify yourself enough to manipulate objects and perform physical attacks. Although you are immune to physical attacks, your body is still a physical object that can be contained, moved, shoved, and otherwise affected by force fields and anything too large to pass through you.

sections.heading: SOLID FORM
sections.text: Self • Power Rank • 2 Hero Points per rank You can turn into solid matter (ice, metal, stone, and wood are always in fashion). While in this form, you can substitute your Power rank for your Might and Toughness, and you gain Armor at that rank as well. If you already have any of these Traits at an equal or greater rank, use their ranks +1d instead.

sections.heading: GESTALT
sections.text: Self • Default Rank • 3 Hero Points You must have the Alter Ego Flaw to select this Power. Assuming you do, your empowered form is the product of two people merging. You have two separate alter egos, each of which is a separate character with their own unique Abilities, Talents, and maybe even Powers. You can have more than two alter egos, but each additional alter ego costs another 3 Hero Points.

sections.heading: GROWTH
sections.text: Self • Power Rank • 1 Hero Point per rank You can grow as large as shown on the Growth table. At rank 4d or higher, your weight rank equals your current Growth rank. You can substitute your current Growth rank for your Might and Toughness. You also gain Armor at your current Growth rank. Last, you gain Running at half your Growth rank thanks to the length of your stride. If you already have any of these Traits at an equal or greater rank, use their ranks +1d instead.
