sections.text: CON −4 Hero Points The Power is always at risk of burning out. Roll two dice every time you try to use it. A roll of 6 or less means the Power burns out and can’t be used for the rest of the scene.

sections.heading: CARRIER ATTACK
sections.text: PRO +6 Hero Points This Pro applies to attack Powers. It means the attack Power carries another Power on its heels, called a carrier attack. The best real-world example of this is a poisoned weapon. Whenever the Power inflicts at least 1 point of damage or 1 page worth of a special effect, you can immediately make a second attack roll against the same target using the carrier attack. Targets can only use passive defenses against a carrier attack. Carrier attacks are expensive: you must buy this Pro and you must by the Power that will serve as the carrier attack. Carrier attacks can’t be used independently. If you want to use a carrier attack by itself, you must buy a second version of the carrier attack Power.

sections.heading: CHARGES
sections.text: CON −1 to −4 Hero Points The Power can only be used a few times per scene. This is a −1 Con if you can use the Power 6 times per scene, a −2 Con if you can use it 3 times per scene, or a −4 Con if you can use it once per scene. The Power is assumed to get recharged, reloaded, or otherwise readied between scenes. Powers with sustained effects like Invisibility or Phasing expend 1 use per page.

sections.heading: CLOSE
sections.text: PRO +2 Hero Points or CON −2 Hero Points This option applies to Touch Powers and Ranged Powers. It means the Power can target subjects within Close Range, even if they are not adjacent to you. This unique option is a +2 Pro when applied to Touch Powers, but a −2 Con when applied to Ranged Powers.

sections.heading: PROS AND CONS
sections.text: Affect Inanimate Ongoing Area of Effect Only Inanimate Armor Piercing Overkill Build-Up Overload Burnout Penetrating Carrier Attack Phase Shift Charges Ranged Close Readied Concentration Recharge Conditional Resisted Constant Ricochet Contagious Selective Costly Shutdown Degrades Side Effect Delay Signature Exclusive Subtle/Undetectable Expansive Sustained Fuse Touch Harmful Toxin Imbue Trap Independent Two-Handed Item Uncontrolled Limited Unreliable Line of Sight Weak

sections.heading: CONCENTRATION
sections.text: CON −4 Hero Points The Power requires your complete attention. Once you use the Power, you can’t perform other actions, move, or defend yourself until your next turn to act. If the Power’s effects last or can be maintained for more than one page, you must keep concentrating or the Power will instantly expire.

sections.heading: CONDITIONAL
sections.text: CON −1 to −4 Hero Points The Power only works under certain conditions, in certain situations, against certain targets, after meeting certain requirements, etc. Considering how difficult it is to satisfy the conditions, this is a −1 Con if the Power often works, a −2 Con if it occasionally works, or a −4 Con if it rarely works.

sections.heading: CONSTANT
sections.text: CON −2 Hero Points This Con applies to Powers that can be activated and deactivated at will. It means the Power is always active and cannot be switched off. This Con is only meaningful when this poses a problem. For example, Aura, Blast, Density, Growth, Invisibility, and Shrinking are all good candidates for this Con.

sections.heading: CONTAGIOUS
sections.text: PRO +4 Hero Points The Power affects not only your original target, but also anyone who comes into physical contact with them. As long as the original target is affected by the Power, you can make an immediate attack roll against anyone who touches them, and these new potential targets can only use passive defenses to resist the Power. New targets affected by the Power also become contagious. This effect always expires at the end of the current scene, at least for Heroes. NPCs have no such restrictions.

sections.heading: COSTLY
sections.text: CON −4 Hero Points You must spend 1 Resolve every time you use the Power. This can represent a Power that takes a great deal out of you, one you have yet to master, or one you are reluctant to use.

sections.heading: DEGRADES
sections.text: CON −2 Hero Points This Con applies to Power Rank Powers and Baseline Rank Powers. It means the Power gets weaker the more you use it. Every use of the Power reduces its effective rank by 1d for the rest of the scene. When this Con applies to ongoing Powers like Aura, every page or fraction of a page is considered one use. All lost ranks are recovered between scenes.

sections.heading: DELAY
sections.text: CON −4 Hero Points The Power doesn’t take effect immediately. Although the length of the delay is up to you (specify when you create the Power), it must be too long for the Power to be of use in combat.

sections.heading: EXCLUSIVE
sections.text: CON −1 Hero Point You can’t use or maintain the Power while you are using or maintaining another Power with this Con, typically because these Powers come from or rely on the same device, energy, source, etc. You must apply this Con to at least 2 of your Powers (and you get the cost reduction for each).

sections.heading: EXPANSIVE
sections.text: PRO +6 to +18 Hero Points This Pro applies to Zone Powers, letting you increase their area of effect dramatically. You can spend 1 Resolve to expand the Power’s area of effect for the rest of the scene. This costs 6 Hero Points if you can affect everything within Close Range (about 50 feet), 12 Hero Points if you can affect everything within Distant Range (about 500 feet), or 18 Hero Points if you can affect everything within Extreme Range (about 5,000 feet). Although not available to Heroes, NPCs can have a Geographic version of this Pro that can affect as large an area as the GM deems appropriate. You cannot apply this Pro to Powers that affect targets directly like Dazzle or Shockwave, but indirect Powers like Darkness, Illusions, Irritant, Light, Nullify, Slick, and Time Stop are perfectly valid.

sections.heading: FUSE
sections.text: PRO +2 Hero Points You can set the Power to take effect after a delay. This delay can be as short or as long as you wish, but not longer than a number of hours equal to your Willpower. You decide how long you want the delay to last each time you use the Power. As long as you are within Extreme Range of where you set the Power to go off or take effect, you can deactivate it at will.

sections.heading: HARMFUL
sections.text: CON −1 to −4 Hero Points You suffer damage every time you use the Power. This is a −1 Con if the Power inflicts 1 point of damage per use, a −2 Con if it inflicts 1–3 points of damage per use (roll one die and halve the result), or a −4 Con if it inflicts 1–6 points of damage per use. You are always free to spend 1 Resolve to avoid suffering this damage. This damage is considered subdual damage, but it ignores the Regeneration Power and can’t be healed with ordinary medical treatment.

sections.heading: IMBUE
sections.text: PRO +4 Hero Points This Pro applies to Powers that only affect you. It means you can also use the Power on other characters and/or objects (whatever makes sense for the Power). You must touch whatever you want to imbue with the Power. Your Willpower equals the maximum number of subjects you can affect at the same time. You can’t affect anything with a weight rank greater than your Willpower.

sections.heading: INDEPENDENT
sections.text: PRO +6 Hero Points The Power has a mind of its own, like a homing missile or a mechanical tentacle that can act of its own accord. The Power can operate like a separate character whenever you wish, acting when you do and using its rank to make any necessary challenge rolls. Although this leaves you free to take other actions without penalty, you can’t use the Power on any page in which it acts independently.

sections.heading: ITEM
sections.text: CON −1 Hero Point The Power comes from an item you carry or wear. Objects implanted into your body are not considered items for these purposes. When you apply this Con to a Power, you must decide whether the item is mundane or unbreakable. Mundane items can be damaged or destroyed, but they can also be repaired or replaced without too much trouble. Unbreakable items are almost impossible to damage or destroy, but they must be recovered if lost, stolen, or taken from you. You must also decide if others can use the item; there are advantages and disadvantages either way. When this Con is applied to an Ability or Talent, its rank drops to 2d if the item is taken away or stops working, but you are free to spend Hero Points to raise the Trait’s default rank above this 2d baseline.

sections.heading: LIMITED
sections.text: CON −1 to −4 Hero Points The Power is less effective, potent, or useful than usual. This is a −1 Con if the Power is somewhat limited, a −2 Con if it’s significantly limited, or a −4 Con if it’s severely limited. Use this Con as a catch-all when nothing else seems appropriate.

sections.heading: LINE OF SIGHT
sections.text: PRO +2 to +6 Hero Points The Power can affect targets at Extreme Range. This is a +2 Pro when applied to Powers that can be used at Distant Range, a +4 Pro when applied to Powers that can be used at Close Range, or a +6 Pro when applied to Powers that require physical contact (Touch Powers). This Pro can’t be applied to Martial Arts, but it can be applied to Strike (Throw) as a +4 Pro. When this Pro is applied to a Zone Power, the Power’s area of effect no longer needs to be centered on the character using it.

sections.heading: ONGOING
sections.text: PRO +6 Hero Points This Pro applies to Powers that inflict damage. It means the Power keeps inflicting damage after the initial attack, doing 1 extra point of damage at the beginning of the following page and continuing for a number of pages equal to the damage inflicted by the original attack. For example, if you hit a target with an ongoing attack and inflict 3 points of damage, the target will take 1 extra point of damage at the start of each of the next 3 pages. This effect isn’t cumulative over multiple attacks: you always inflict only 1 point of damage per page, and you always use only the longest effective duration. Targets can spend 1 Resolve or forego their next turn to act to rid themselves of all ongoing attacks affecting them.

sections.heading: ONLY INANIMATE
sections.text: CON −1 to −4 Hero Points This Pro applies to Powers that only affect living beings. It means the Power affects inanimate beings instead. This is a −1 Con if you can affect characters with the Inanimate Power from any Source, a −2 Con if you can affect characters with the Inanimate Power from 2 Sources (pick them), or a −4 Con if you can affect characters with the Inanimate Power from one Source (pick one).

sections.heading: OVERKILL
sections.text: CON (Special) The Power is more damaging or potent than it is accurate. As a result, targets double the total number of successes rolled when using an active defense to resist the Power in combat. This unusual Con reduces a Power’s base cost by 1 Hero Point per rank (or changes its base cost from 1 Hero Point per rank to 1 Hero Point per 2 ranks). As noted earlier, this Con can also be applied to Might. Aside from being ordinary Cons, Overkill and its opposite Weak (see below) are tools GMs can use to regulate their games and balance characters of disparate power levels. Consider the following examples: GMs who want to expand how powerful Heroes can be without raising the game’s Trait Cap may let Heroes have higher Trait ranks if they use the Overkill or Weak Cons. When using this optional rule, a Trait with either Con can exceed the Trait Cap by up to 3 ranks in games with a Trait Cap of at least 9d or by up to 6 ranks in games with a Trait Cap of at least 18d. Conversely, GMs who want to limit how powerful Heroes can be without lowering the game’s Trait Cap may rule that all Traits of a certain rank or higher must have either Overkill or Weak if they inflict damage. The rank that triggers this requirement is up to the GM, but it should never be lower than 9d.

sections.heading: OVERLOAD
sections.text: PRO +2 Hero Points You can overload the Power, increasing its effective rank but burning it out in the process. You can increase the Power’s rank by 3d or 6d for one page. If you increase it by 3d, you lose the Power for the rest of the scene. If you increase it by 6d, you lose the Power for the rest of the issue. If this Pro is applied to a Variant Power or to the original Power on which a Variant is based, it burns out the original Power and all Variants (whether or not they have this Pro) when used.

sections.heading: PENETRATING
sections.text: PRO +4 Hero Points This Pro applies to Powers that inflict physical or energy damage, and means they cut through physical objects like a hot knife through butter. Passive defenses are halved against the Power. Force fields are the exception; a target protected by the Force Field Power is immune to this effect. Active defenses are unaffected by this Pro. No Power can have this Pro and the Weak Con.

sections.heading: PHASE SHIFT
sections.text: PRO +4 Hero Points The Power affects insubstantial and incorporeal targets as if they were solid. For example, characters using Powers like Gaseous Form, Liquid Form, and Phasing are considered solid when targeted by the Power. This also works in reverse, meaning that characters who are incorporeal (those using Phasing) can use the Power against ordinary solid targets. GMs are free to prohibit Heroes who can become incorporeal from using this Pro since it allows them to affect the physical world while remaining immune to physical attacks and effects. Of course, NPCs are not subject to this restriction.

sections.heading: RANGED
sections.text: PRO +2 or +4 Hero Points The Power can affect targets at Distant Range. This is a +2 Pro when applied to Powers that can be used at Close Range or a +4 Pro when applied to Powers that require physical contact (Touch Powers). This Pro can’t be applied to Martial Arts, but it can be applied to Strike (Throw) as a +2 Pro. When this Pro is applied to a Zone Power, the Power’s area of effect no longer needs to be centered on the character using it.

sections.heading: READIED
sections.text: CON −2 Hero Points The Power must be readied between each use. You must spend 1 page to ready the Power, but if you spend 1 Resolve, you can do it in 1 action instead. Whether or not you spend Resolve, you can move and perform free actions while readying the Power.

sections.heading: RECHARGE
sections.text: CON −4 Hero Points The Power must recharge between uses. It can only be used once every 3 pages. In other words, once you use the Power, you can’t use it again for the next 2 pages.

sections.heading: RESISTED
sections.text: PRO +6 Hero Points This Pro applies to Powers that inflict special effects and can be resisted with active defenses. It means the Power never misses or doesn’t need to make contact. As a result, targets cannot use active defenses to resist the Power. This Pro is always subject to the GM’s approval.

sections.heading: RICOCHET
sections.text: PRO +2 Hero Points This Pro applies to ranged attack Powers. It means you can bank the Power off multiple surfaces, letting you target enemies around corners or behind cover without suffering a penalty to your attack rolls. Additionally you can spend 1 Resolve to defeat twice as many as Minions usual, or 2 per net success rolled, by bouncing the Power off multiple enemies—this provides no additional benefit to attacks that already work this way (i.e., area attacks, Super Speed attacks, and Two-Fisted attacks). You can decide whether to spend Resolve after making your attack roll.

sections.heading: SELECTIVE
sections.text: PRO +4 Hero Points The Power will not harm or affect anyone you don’t want harmed or affected. If the Power can be used to perform area attacks or has an Area of Effect Pro, you can spend 1 Resolve whenever you make an area attack to target only select individuals in the area of effect.

sections.heading: SHUTDOWN
sections.text: CON −1 to −4 Hero Points Either the Power can’t affect a person or object it should be able to affect, or something can prevent the Power from working and/or shut it down. Considering how often the Power is impaired, this is a −1 Con if the Power often works, a −2 Con if it occasionally works, or a −4 Con if it rarely works.

sections.heading: SIDE EFFECT
sections.text: CON −1 to −4 Hero Points The Power has a detrimental side effect such as causing collateral damage, creating a terrible smell, killing nearby plant life, etc. The side effect must be more than the obvious effect of the Power. For example, all area attacks cause collateral damage, so that can’t be a side effect for a typical area attack Power. This is a −1 Con if the side effect is annoying or inconvenient, a −2 Con if the side effect is detrimental or harmful, or a −4 Con if the side effect is catastrophic or debilitating.

sections.heading: SIGNATURE
sections.text: CON −1 Hero Point The Power leaves a residue, energy signature, or something else that can be detected by anyone who knows what to look for and traced back to you. Describe the specifics when you apply this Con.

sections.heading: SUBTLE/UNDETECTABLE
sections.text: PRO +2 or +6 Hero Points Subtle is a +2 Pro that means the Power creates no loud noise, bright light, nor anything else that can easily be detected from a distance. Undetectable is a +6 Pro that means the Power can’t be detected or traced back to you, at least not by ordinary senses. It also means you give no indication when using the Power. For example, you can use Telekinesis (Undetectable) to grab a purse snatcher and hold them in the air until the police arrive while appearing to be nothing more than an ordinary person sitting at an outdoor café minding their own business. Targets suffer a −3d penalty to their active defense rolls against Undetectable physical and energy attacks unless they have a Power like Blind Fighting that compensates for this. GMs are well within their rights to prohibit Heroes from using Undetectable.

sections.heading: SUSTAINED
sections.text: CON −2 Hero Points This Con applies to Powers that last or can be maintained for some amount of time. It means you must spend 1 action per page sustaining the Power. If not, the Power instantly expires.

sections.heading: TOUCH
sections.text: CON −2 or −4 Hero Points The Power requires physical contact. This is a −2 Con when applied to Powers that can be used at Close Range or a −4 Con when applied to Powers that can be used at Distant Range.

sections.heading: TOXIN
sections.text: CON −2 Hero Points The Power represents a disease, drug, or poison. It can’t affect characters who are immune to toxins, and targets can use the Resistance Power as a passive defense against the Power.

sections.heading: TRAP
sections.text: PRO +2 Hero Points You can trap an area or object with the Power. Once set, the trap is triggered by anyone who enters the area or handles the object incorrectly (or at all). Powers that affect others use their rank to make any necessary attack rolls when triggered. Each trap can run up to 15 feet long, cover an area up to 5 feet in diameter (or a single 5-foot by 5-foot square), or affect an object small enough to fit into this space. You can always trap a small part of a large object. Your Willpower equals the maximum number of traps you can have set at any time. Traps that have not been triggered vanish at the end of the current issue.

sections.heading: TWO-HANDED
sections.text: CON −1 Hero Points You need both hands free to use the Power. This often means you must gesture with both hands or the Power comes from an object or weapon you wield in both hands.

sections.heading: UNCONTROLLED
sections.text: CON −2 Hero Points This Con applies to Powers that can be activated and deactivated at will. It means the Power always activates in certain situations. You have no control over this and can’t stop it from happening. This Con is only meaningful when the specific circumstances are problematic.

sections.heading: UNRELIABLE
sections.text: CON −2 Hero Points The Power sometimes fails to work. Roll two dice every time you try to use it. A roll of 6 or less means the Power doesn’t work and you waste your action. You can try again on the following page.

sections.heading: WEAK
sections.text: CON (Special) The Power is more accurate than it is damaging or potent. As a result, targets double the total number of successes rolled when using a passive defense to resist the Power in combat. This unusual Con reduces a Power’s base cost by 1 Hero Point per rank (or changes its base cost from 1 Hero Point per rank to 1 Hero Point per 2 ranks). No Power can have this Con and the Armor Piercing or Penetrating Pros.

sections.heading: PERKS
sections.text: Perks are advantages that come from the world around you. Like many of the Powers, Perks are generic and need to be fleshed out when selected. As social characteristics, Perks are more narrative than mechanical in nature. Perks don’t have ranks or Sources and don’t take Pros or Cons. Feel free to make up your own Perks using the ones provided below as a guide.

sections.heading: AUTHORITY
sections.text: Perk • 3 Hero Points You have more authority, rights, or social power than the average person. This could include things like access to secret government installations, diplomatic immunity, top secret security clearance, authority to arrest and detain people, or just being a member of the nobility or ruling class.

sections.heading: CONTACTS
sections.text: Perk • 1 Hero Point per type of contact You know people who can provide you with information and the occasional favor. Common examples include academic, business, criminal, legal, media, military, police, political, and scientific contacts.

sections.heading: FAME
sections.text: Perk • 3 Hero Points You are famous. People who recognize you generally react favorably, and some will fall all over themselves trying to get your attention, an autograph, or a selfie with you. If you have a secret identity, you must decide whether this Perk applies to your civilian identity or your heroic alter ego.

sections.heading: FOURTH WALL
sections.text: Perk • 6 Hero Points You believe you are a character in a comic book (and you might be right). You often break the fourth wall to interact directly with the audience. In game terms, any time you break the fourth wall and crack a joke that gets everyone at the table laughing, you earn 1 point of Resolve. But you can only do this once per scene. This Perk is best reserved for comedic or lighthearted games.

sections.heading: HEADQUARTERS
sections.text: Perk • 1 Hero Point per 3 Base Points You have a base of operations or headquarters of some kind. Every Hero Point you spend on this Perk gives you 3 Base Points to spend on your headquarters. Multiple Heroes can apply their Base Points to the same headquarters. You can find rules for creating headquarters in Chapter 6.

sections.heading: INFAMY
sections.text: Perk • 3 Hero Points You are infamous among the criminal underworld, known as a dangerous customer and someone to be feared. Ordinary criminals are afraid of you and may fall all over themselves trying to appease you, especially when you apply the right kind of pressure. Supervillains are usually less impressed.

sections.heading: PATRON
sections.text: Perk • 3 Hero Points You are connected to a person, group, or organization that provides you with information, equipment, funding, and support for your heroic activities. Common patrons include government organizations, rebel groups, and wealthy humanitarians who just love adopting teenagers with superpowers.

sections.heading: PET/SIDEKICK
sections.text: Perk • 1 Hero Point per 10 Hero Points You have a pet or a sidekick. Every Hero Point you spend on this Perk gives you 10 Hero Points to create this character. Your companion can’t have more than half your Hero Points, and they must abide by the game’s Trait Cap. Your companion earns 1 Hero Point for every 2 that you earn. Pets and sidekicks are considered Heroes. They lack Resolve, but you can spend your Resolve on their behalf. If your companion has higher Trait ranks than you, use their Traits when determining your Resolve (see Chapter 5). If your companion has Flaws, you earn Resolve as if that character were a Hero. GMs who don’t want players running two (or more) characters should feel free to limit or prohibit this Perk.

sections.heading: REPUTATION
sections.text: Perk • 3 Hero Points You have a reputation that works to your benefit. Unlike fame, which makes people like you, this Perk means you have authority, credibility, or respect in a particular arena. For example, in your civilian life, you might be an attorney known to be an absolute terror in the courtroom. If you have a secret identity, you must decide whether this Perk applies to your civilian identity or your heroic alter ego.

sections.heading: RESOURCES
sections.text: Perk • 1 Hero Point You have access to an impressive supply of equipment of one sort or another: military weapons, ninja gear, tricked-out vehicles, etc. This often means you know someone who gets you these things or you stumbled across a hidden cache. It does not mean you are rich. For that, see Wealth.

sections.heading: PERKS
sections.text: Authority Patron Contacts Pet/Sidekick Fame Reputation Fourth Wall Resources Headquarters Unique Vehicle Infamy Wealth/Great Wealth

sections.heading: UNIQUE VEHICLE
sections.text: Perk • 1 Hero Point per 25 Vehicle Points You have one or more unique vehicles. Every Hero Point you spend on this Perk gives you 25 Vehicle Points to spend on your vehicles. Rules for creating unique vehicles are in Chapter 6.

sections.heading: WEALTH/GREAT WEALTH
sections.text: Perk • 3 or 6 Hero Points Wealth costs 3 Hero Points and means you are rich. You aren’t just comfortably well-off; you are truly wealthy. You can buy almost anything you want, legal or otherwise. You probably own several homes, have multiple vehicles, and employ at least a few domestic servants. If you happen to be a tech-based Hero, you can easily fund your extracurricular activities out of your own pocket. Great Wealth costs 6 Hero Points and means you are one of the wealthiest people in the world. At this level, money is almost meaningless. Not only can you buy whatever you want, but you can spend 1 point of Resolve once per issue to make a truly absurd purchase like buying an island or a major corporation. While many Heroes are wealthy, GMs may want to restrict Great Wealth because characters with this much money can spend their way around most problems without batting an eye.

sections.heading: FLAWS
sections.text: Flaws are physical, mental, and social hindrances. As noted earlier, all Heroes can have up to 3 Flaws and must have at least one. The following section includes several Flaws common to the superhero genre, but feel free to make up your own (after discussing them with your GM). Flaws not only make your Hero more interesting; they also help you earn Resolve. Whenever you find yourself in a situation where one of your Flaws could become an issue, you can bring it into play by describing what happens. If this makes things more difficult for you or your fellow Heroes, you earn 1 point of Resolve. Your Flaws are always under your control and come into play only when you decide. No Flaw can generate more than 1 Resolve per scene. Although most Flaws work as described above, there are two exceptions. Some Flaws like Enemy and Relationship are plot hooks for GMs to use however they wish. Others like Blind and Vulnerability are persistent conditions that can’t be resisted and are always in effect. These Flaws are sometimes called Plot Hooks and Conditions, respectively, and they aren’t under your control. You don’t bring Plot Hooks or Conditions into play to earn Resolve. Instead, these Flaws grant you 1 extra point of Resolve at the start of every issue, and that’s it. They come into play whenever the GM decides or the situation demands, and you don’t gain extra Resolve when that happens.

sections.heading: NPC FLAWS
sections.text: Flaws work differently for NPCs. NPCs often have less than 3 Flaws, and sometimes have none. That’s because, unlike Heroes, NPCs always succumb to their Flaws. For example, a Villain with the Fear (heights) Flaw will always avoid open balconies, ledges, etc. The only way for an NPC to overcome a Flaw is with Adversity. Once per scene, the GM can spend 1 Adversity to have an NPC resist a Flaw for the rest of that scene (and no NPC can resist the same Flaw more than once per issue). This also applies to friendly NPCs, but in this case, it costs Resolve instead of Adversity (a Hero must spend the Resolve). For these reasons, NPCs usually have Flaws that are always in effect or triggered by a particular person, object, situation, etc., and the specifics must be described in detail when the NPC is created. Flaws that don’t have a concrete effect on a character’s interactions with Heroes are usually ignored or added purely for descriptive purposes. The same goes for Flaws that don’t come up very often, mainly affect the character’s personal life, or take effect off-screen. Unless otherwise noted in a character’s write-up, Flaws like these are merely descriptive when applied to NPCs. While they may occasionally come up in play, their effects are entirely up to the GM. The following Flaws are assumed to be merely descriptive when applied to NPCs: Absentminded, Alter Ego, Amnesia, Broke, Clumsy, Color Blind, Creepy, Decorum, Emotionless, Enemy, Finite Power, Frightening, Hidden Agenda, Illiterate, Impaired Sense, Insane, Light Sensitive, Nocturnal, Notoriety, Obligation, Outsider, Quirk, Relationship, Restriction, Secret, Secret Identity, Slow, Unlucky/Jinx, and Wanted. This isn’t to say these Flaws aren’t real or have no effect on NPCs. It only means that their impact is completely up to the GM. If the GM wants any of these Flaws to have a specific mechanical effect, they have to describe it in detail on a case-by-case basis.

sections.heading: ABSENTMINDED
sections.text: You tend to forget things. Usually, the things you forget aren’t all that important. But sometimes they are. Whenever that happens, you earn a point of Resolve.

sections.heading: ALTER EGO
sections.text: You have a mundane alter ego. Your alter ego is built with 50 Hero Points and earns 1 Hero Point for every 5 you earn. Decide how your transformation works and whether it has any limitations when you select this Flaw. Any time this causes you trouble, you earn a point of Resolve.

sections.heading: AMNESIA
sections.text: You have no memory of your past, although you may be haunted by fragments in dreams or visions. You don’t know who you are or where you come from. People who know this can take advantage of you, and your past will come back to haunt you every so often. This Flaw is both a Plot Hook and a Condition, so it grants you 1 extra point of Resolve at the start of every issue.

sections.heading: AVERSION/FEAR
sections.text: You have an aversion to or fear of something, and you will do whatever you can to avoid it. If you can’t, you may become hysterical, nauseated, violent, or worse. You may even pass out. However it works, you earn a point of Resolve whenever you succumb to this Flaw. Common fears include a fear of the dark, enclosed spaces, fire, heights, insects, mice, public speaking, snakes, spiders, and water.

sections.heading: BEAST
sections.text: Your mental faculties are about on par with a bright animal or a game designer. You act mostly on instinct, and complex reasoning is beyond you. You earn a point of Resolve any time you can’t figure out how to do things like open a door or get the sheriff to understand that Billy fell down a well.

sections.heading: BLIND/DEAF
sections.text: You are completely blind or deaf (pick one). If you are blind, you may have to select at least one Power that compensates enough to let you operate as a superhero (discuss this with your GM). This Flaw is a Condition that grants you 1 extra point of Resolve at the start of every issue.

sections.heading: BROKE
sections.text: You are penniless, jobless, and possibly homeless. You can’t buy anything, so you have to beg, borrow, or steal what you need. Every time this causes you problems, you earn a point of Resolve.

sections.heading: CLUMSY
sections.text: For whatever reason, you tend to break things. Your allies know to keep the fragile stuff away from you. Nevertheless, accidents happen. When they do, you earn a point of Resolve.

sections.heading: CODE
sections.text: You follow a rigid code of conduct, one that requires more of you than just acting heroically. You earn a point of Resolve whenever following your code hurts you or your allies.

sections.heading: COLOR BLIND
sections.text: You see in black and white, or you have trouble distinguishing certain colors (reds and greens being the usual culprits). You earn a point of Resolve whenever this causes you problems.

sections.heading: COMPULSION/SEVERE COMPULSION
sections.text: You have trouble resisting the urge to do something like drinking, gambling, chasing potential romantic partners, grandstanding, proving that your intellect is unmatched, or working on that stupid roleplaying game all night long. You earn a point of Resolve any time this works to your detriment. If the compulsion is literally impossible to resist, then you have a Severe Compulsion, which is a Condition that grants you 1 extra point of Resolve at the start of every issue. If you have a Severe Compulsion, you must describe the specific environment, situation, etc. that triggers the compulsion.

sections.heading: CREEPY
sections.text: You give off a vibe that unnerves sensitive observers like young children, psychics, and animals. Animals usually shy away from you, unless they’re predators, in which case they attack you first. You earn a point of Resolve whenever your unsettling aura causes you trouble.

sections.heading: CURSE
sections.text: You suffer from some supernatural burden. Make up the details and get your GM’s approval. You earn a point of Resolve whenever your curse causes problems for you or your allies.

sections.heading: DECORUM
sections.text: You value propriety and feel compelled to follow social mores, even when others don’t. Manners maketh man, and all that. Whenever this makes life difficult, you earn a point of Resolve.

sections.heading: DISABLED
sections.text: You are disabled, possibly missing a limb or two, possibly wheelchair-bound, possibly something else. Describe the specifics when you select this Flaw. You may have to select at least one Power that compensates enough to let you operate as a superhero (discuss this with your GM). This Flaw is a Condition that grants you 1 extra point of Resolve at the start of every issue.

sections.heading: FLAWS
sections.text: Absentminded Impaired Sense Alter Ego Insane Amnesia Light Sensitive Aversion/Fear Mute Beast Night Blind Blind/Deaf Nocturnal Broke Notoriety Clumsy Obligation Code Outsider Color Blind Power Limits Compulsion (Severe) Quirk Creepy Reaction (Severe) Curse Relationship Decorum Repair Disabled Requirement (Severe) Emotionless Restriction Enemy Secret Finite Power Secret Identity Flashbacks/Guilt Slow Frenzy Unlucky/Jinx Frightening Unusual Looks Heavy/Very Heavy Unusual Shape Hidden Agenda Vulnerability Illiterate Wanted

sections.heading: EMOTIONLESS
sections.text: You lack human empathy. Unable to understand emotions, you are often coldly logical in your interactions with others. As a result, people tend to react poorly to even your most carefully reasoned attempts at meaningful exchange. You earn a point of Resolve any time this causes you problems.

sections.heading: ENEMY
sections.text: You have an enemy that wants you ruined, imprisoned, or dead. Make up whatever details you want and let your GM make up the rest. Your enemy doesn’t necessarily have to be a single individual or a super-powered nemesis. It could instead be a group, an organization, or even an entire nation. This Flaw is a Plot Hook that grants you 1 extra point of Resolve at the start of every issue.

sections.heading: FINITE POWER
sections.text: One or more of your Powers requires ammo, energy, or some other depletable resource. You earn a point of Resolve whenever you run out of this resource at the wrong time.

sections.heading: FLASHBACKS/GUILT
sections.text: You are haunted by some tragic event in your past. Whenever something triggers you, you suffer flashbacks or become overwhelmed with guilt, sorrow, etc. Flashbacks take you completely out of the action and render you helpless for 1 page. Being overwhelmed with guilt causes you to suffer a −2d penalty to all challenge rolls for 3 pages. Either way, you also earn a point of Resolve.

sections.heading: FRENZY
sections.text: You tend to rush headlong into combat and often go dangerously berserk. You earn a point of Resolve whenever this gets the better of you and makes you do something stupid like leap blindly into a fight, refuse to retreat with your allies, or kill someone in the heat of battle.

sections.heading: FRIGHTENING
sections.text: You look downright scary. Most people flee in terror when they see you, and those who don’t are often on edge in your presence. You earn a point of Resolve whenever this causes you problems.

sections.heading: HEAVY/VERY HEAVY
sections.text: You weigh a good bit more than the average person. If you have a weight rank of 5d or 6d, you are Heavy. You can’t ride most mounts, and you are probably a poor swimmer at best. You earn a point of Resolve whenever your weight becomes an issue. If you have a weight rank of 7d or greater, you are Very Heavy, heavy enough to damage floors and crash through ceilings. At this level, you have a Condition that grants you 1 extra point of Resolve at the start of every issue.

sections.heading: HIDDEN AGENDA
sections.text: You sometimes have directives or goals you can’t/won’t discuss with your allies. Whenever your hidden agenda gets in the way or makes things difficult for you or your allies, you earn a point of Resolve.

sections.heading: ILLITERATE
sections.text: You cannot read or write, at least not any language known on present-day Earth. You earn a point of Resolve whenever this hampers you in a significant way.

sections.heading: IMPAIRED SENSE
sections.text: Your hearing, smell, or vision is lousy—pick one or more, whatever you prefer. You earn a point of Resolve whenever you choose to automatically fail a Perception roll as a result of your impairment and your failure has some adverse consequence for you or your allies.

sections.heading: INSANE
sections.text: You suffer from a persistent behavioral issue, delusion, or disconnect with reality or you endure occasional psychotic breaks in the form of hallucinations, bouts of paranoia, etc. Whenever your illness causes you problems, you earn a point of Resolve. If you take medication that keeps you in check, consider taking Requirement instead.

sections.heading: LIGHT SENSITIVE
sections.text: You are sensitive to bright light. You might be an albino, but that doesn’t have to be the case. Simple daylight can be blinding, and prolonged exposure can make you dizzy or incapacitate you. You earn a point of Resolve any time you suffer an adverse effect because of this condition.

sections.heading: MUTE
sections.text: You can’t speak, won’t speak, or speak a language nobody else understands (although maybe another Hero can translate for you). Any time this creates challenges for your or your allies, you earn 1 Resolve. This Flaw doesn’t prevent you from speaking to your fellow players or the GM; it only prevents your Hero from speaking to other characters in the game world.

sections.heading: NIGHT BLIND
sections.text: You have a hard time seeing in dim lighting, which is almost like darkness to you. You earn a point of Resolve any time you suffer an adverse effect because of this condition.

sections.heading: NOCTURNAL
sections.text: You are wired to sleep during the day, or you have a form of narcolepsy. Either way, you tend to be tired and sluggish during the day, and you sometimes doze off when things are calm—shaving cream beards are all too familiar. Whenever this becomes an issue, you earn a point of Resolve.

sections.heading: NOTORIETY
sections.text: Whether deserved or not, you have a bad reputation. Maybe you’ve become the target of a newspaper editor who hates “costumed freaks.” Perhaps you used to be a supervillain and the public hasn’t forgiven or forgotten. Or you might be the unfortunate subject of blind prejudice. Whatever the case, most people react unfavorably to you. Some may even flee or call the police when you appear. When things like this happen, you sigh and earn a point of Resolve.

sections.heading: OBLIGATION
sections.text: You have a duty or responsibility that requires you to do certain things and prevents you from doing others. Being a student and having a full-time job are common Obligations on present-day Earth. This Flaw is a Plot Hook that grants you 1 extra point of Resolve at the start of every issue.

sections.heading: OUTSIDER
sections.text: You come from somewhere else, often another time, world, or dimension. Your home is quite different from present-day Earth, so there are bound to be faux pas and missteps. You earn a point of Resolve any time you have trouble dealing with novel objects or situations.

sections.heading: POWER LIMITS
sections.text: One or more of your Powers has certain limitations. Describe the specifics. In effect, this works like a Con that you control, but instead of making the Power less expensive, this Flaw lets you earn 1 point of Resolve whenever this works to your detriment or to that of your allies.

sections.heading: QUIRK
sections.text: You have an annoying, obnoxious, or unfortunate personality trait that often gets the better of you at the worst of times. You earn a point of Resolve whenever that happens.

sections.heading: REACTION/SEVERE REACTION
sections.text: You suffer an adverse reaction at certain times, in certain situations, or when you touch or come within a certain distance of a specific person, place, or thing. Make up the details when you select this Flaw. However it works, you earn a point of Resolve whenever you suffer a reaction, or when you do something selfish or unheroic to avoid whatever causes your reaction. If your reaction is especially severe and impossible to resist, like how sunlight burns vampires, then you have a Severe Reaction, which is a Condition that grants you 1 extra point of Resolve at the start of every issue.

sections.heading: RELATIONSHIP
sections.text: You have important relationships in your life, often your friends and family (and maybe even pets). These people and/or animals require your attention and occasionally need your help, sometimes to rescue them from the clutches of some Villain, and sometimes for other reasons. This common Flaw is a Plot Hook that grants you 1 extra point of Resolve at the start of every issue.

sections.heading: REPAIR
sections.text: You do not heal naturally. Whenever you suffer damage, you must be repaired to recover lost Health, whether that happens magically, mechanically, or in some other way. This Flaw is a Condition that grants you 1 extra point of Resolve at the start of every issue.

sections.heading: REQUIREMENT/SEVERE REQUIREMENT
sections.text: You must satisfy a requirement every so often or you will suffer an adverse effect. Maybe you have to perform a nightly ritual to maintain your powers, or you need regular doses of medicine to stay alive, or perhaps you are addicted to alcohol, drugs, or gambling. Make up the details when you select this Flaw. You earn a point of Resolve whenever you do something selfish or unheroic to satisfy the requirement, or when you suffer an adverse effect from not satisfying the requirement. If the requirement is desperate and immediate, like breathing water instead of air, then you have a Severe Requirement, which is a Condition that grants you 1 extra point of Resolve at the start of every issue.

sections.heading: RESTRICTION
sections.text: You have fewer rights than the average person, often because you are a minor or an undocumented alien (maybe literally). This also applies if you are a second-class citizen, were deemed legally incompetent, etc. Whenever your restriction makes things difficult, you earn a point of Resolve.

sections.heading: SECRET
sections.text: You have a secret that must be kept at all costs. You earn a point of Resolve whenever your efforts to protect your secret work to your detriment or to the detriment of your allies.

sections.heading: SECRET IDENTITY
sections.text: This is the iconic version of the Secret Flaw in most comic book superhero settings.

sections.heading: SLOW
sections.text: You move slowly. You earn a point of Resolve whenever you choose to automatically fail an Agility roll involving speed or movement and the failure has negative consequences for you or your allies. This Flaw is almost meaningless if you have a Travel Power that compensates for it.

sections.heading: UNLUCKY/JINX
sections.text: If it weren’t for bad luck, you wouldn’t have any luck at all. Unlucky means the GM can inflict a misfortune on you once per issue without needing to spend Adversity (for more on this, see Chapter 5). Jinx works the same way, but the misfortune affects a fellow Hero or ally in your vicinity instead of you. This Flaw is a Condition that grants you 1 extra point of Resolve at the start of every issue.

sections.heading: UNUSUAL LOOKS
sections.text: Your appearance is off-putting. You might look incredibly ugly, unnaturally beautiful, or strange and uncanny in some other way. Whatever the case, you earn a point of Resolve whenever your appearance becomes an issue. This Flaw is redundant if you have Frightening.

sections.heading: UNUSUAL SHAPE
sections.text: You are not shaped like an ordinary human being. Describe how you are shaped and how this affects you when you select this Flaw. Whenever this causes you problems, you earn a point of Resolve.

sections.heading: VULNERABILITY
sections.text: You are vulnerable to one type of attack, effect, or weapon. Describe it in detail when you select this Flaw. Your active and passive defense ranks are halved against this attack, effect, or weapon. This Flaw is a Condition that grants you 1 extra point of Resolve at the start of every issue.

sections.heading: WANTED
sections.text: On a steel horse you ride. You are being actively hunted by authorities of some kind, so your hand is often forced in order to avoid being discovered, or to escape in those instances when you are. This Flaw is a Plot Hook that grants you 1 extra point of Resolve at the start of every issue.

sections.heading: DERIVED CHARACTERISTICS
sections.text: To avoid having to look these things up during the game, you should now determine your Edge, Health, and Resolve. Edge and Health are described in Chapter 4. Resolve is discussed at length in Chapter 5.

sections.heading: EDGE
sections.text: Your Edge equals your Perception plus the greater of your Agility or Intellect. Note that certain Powers like Danger Sense, Lightning Reflexes, and Super Speed can affect your Edge.

sections.heading: HEALTH
sections.text: Your Health equals the average of your Toughness and Might or the average of your Toughness and Willpower. Use whichever option gives you the most Health. When creating a Foe, use half this value. As discussed later in these rules, this is more a suggestion than a rule when dealing with NPCs.

sections.heading: RESOLVE
sections.text: Your Resolve depends on how close your Ability ranks and Power ranks come to the game’s Trait Cap. Turn to Chapter 5 to determine your Resolve. Note that the Determination Power and certain Flaws (Plot Hooks and Conditions) grant you extra starting Resolve. Only Heroes have Resolve.

sections.heading: FINISHING TOUCHES
sections.text: Now that you have your Abilities, Talents, Powers, Perks, and Flaws, you get to add your finishing touches. These are the descriptive elements that turn a collection of game mechanics into a living, breathing character in the game world. Your finishing touches include your name and civilian identity, a description, your motivation, a quote, three connections, three details, and your origin.

sections.heading: NAME AND IDENTITY
sections.text: Select your superhero name and your actual name, or at least the one you use in your civilian identity. Most Heroes, even those with public identities, tend to use a heroic codename.

sections.heading: DESCRIPTION
sections.text: Describe the three things people first notice about you when they meet you in costume, then describe the three things they first notice when they meet you in everyday civilian attire. Although your costume is obviously important, you can also include things like your personality and demeanor, the way you move or carry yourself, the way you speak (or don’t speak), and so on.

sections.heading: MOTIVATION
sections.text: Not everyone with superpowers would choose to be a superhero. Most people would decide to lead normal lives, free of the troubles and dangers that come with the whole hero gig. But not you; you are different, and your motivation explains why. Although Heroes can have more than one motivation, there’s always one that underlies everything else. Motivations are generic, so two vastly different Heroes can nevertheless share the same motivation. As Heroes mature, their motivations may change.

sections.heading: ADVENTURE
sections.text: You are a superhero for the adventure and excitement of it. You may be young, going through a phase or a mid-life crisis, or one of those people who need to live life on the edge. Of course, there are plenty of ways to get an adrenaline rush, and the fact that you choose to do it in a way that protects others says a great deal about your good-hearted, heroic nature.

sections.heading: ALTRUISM
sections.text: You are a superhero because it’s the only reasonable course of action for you and others like you, at least if you want the world to have any kind of future. You’ve given this a lot of thought, and while you may or may not be especially good or noble, you can’t escape your conclusion. Some Heroes with this motivation have genius-level intelligence, but others are ordinary folks who sat down at the kitchen table trying to figure out what they were going to do after discovering they had superhuman abilities.

sections.heading: CAREER
sections.text: You work as a superhero for the government, military, police, or some other organization. Or maybe you are a hero-for-hire or a private detective with powers, although it can be tough to make ends meet since you can’t seem to turn away anyone who needs your help, even if they can’t pay. You might even be chasing the fame and wealth that comes with being a super-powered celebrity. Whatever the case, you try to balance a no-nonsense levelheadedness with your drive to serve and protect others.

sections.heading: DEVOTION
sections.text: You are a superhero because of someone else. Someone you love is a superhero and you want to impress, protect, act as a mentor, or keep them out of trouble. Or someone you care about needs you to be a superhero, for whatever reason, so here you are. Although this motivation is less altruistic than most, many Heroes who start out with this motivation come to develop an appreciation for doing the right thing and eventually drop this motivation in favor of another.

sections.heading: IDEALISM
sections.text: You are a superhero because you espouse or embody the noblest ideals of a people, group, or nation. You live by your ideals, and through your selfless heroics, you inspire others to do the same. This doesn’t make you a mindless follower, nationalist, or zealot. You believe in the dream, first and foremost, so much so that if the people, group, or nation who once espoused your ideals suddenly turns its back on them, you will be the first to plant yourself firm and say, “No, you move.”

sections.heading: MOTIVATIONS
sections.text: Adventure Knowledge Altruism Nature Career Redemption Devotion Responsibility Idealism Trouble Justice Virtue

sections.heading: JUSTICE
sections.text: The system is supposed to protect people, but that doesn’t always happen. Some crimes are too big or too small. Some criminals are too powerful or too slippery. And some victims are too invisible or too unpopular. When the system fails, it’s up to people like you to fill the gaps, protect the innocent, and right the wrongs. You fight to protect those you can, and to get justice for those you can’t.

sections.heading: KNOWLEDGE
sections.text: You are on a quest for knowledge or spiritual enlightenment, and your heroics arise out of helping those you encounter along the way. Maybe you seek to explore unknown frontiers, invent new technologies, or push science and human understanding to new horizons. Maybe you are looking inward, learning to tap your infinite potential, or trying to understand yourself and your place in the universe. You might even be an alien or a robot trying to understand what it means to be human.

sections.heading: NATURE
sections.text: You are a superhero because that’s what your instincts tell you to be—it’s in your DNA or hardwired into your programming. You might be a noble beast whose natural instincts lead you to acts of heroism. You could be insane, disconnected from reality, but your actions always have you on the side of the angels. Or you could be a construct of some kind, like a robot or clockwork soldier, programmed for heroism.

sections.heading: REDEMPTION
sections.text: You have made mistakes, and now you are trying to redeem yourself. Your need for redemption might be internal, the desire to make amends for your past, or it might be external, a promise offered in exchange for forgiveness or leniency. At least it might have started that way, with you coerced into this life, until you woke up one morning and realized this is who you were meant to be all along.

sections.heading: RESPONSIBILITY
sections.text: You have abilities and powers that most don’t, and you have a duty to use them for the good of others. Maybe this is how you were raised, or maybe this was recently made clear to you. You could have a heroic obligation of some kind, a legacy to live up to. Or maybe you just have a deep respect for the value of law and order in a civil society. You act out of a sense of duty and take being a superhero seriously.

sections.heading: TROUBLE
sections.text: You have a problem, one you can’t solve on your own, so you sought the assistance of other superheroes or their patron. Maybe you developed powers you need to learn to control. Perhaps you were dying, and your powers are the byproduct of some magical or technological process that saved your life. Maybe you need super-powered help to save someone you love, or to protect yourself from someone or something. Maybe you were coerced into being a superhero, or at least you were at first. Or perhaps you just want to find a place where you’ll be accepted rather than seen as a freak or a monster.

sections.heading: VIRTUE
sections.text: You are a superhero because it’s the right thing to do. People are supposed to do what they can to help each other. Your special abilities let you do more than most, so you do. It’s that simple. An optimist, you will never stop fighting for the dignity and freedom of every human being. If you didn’t have superpowers, you would find another way to work for the good of others.

sections.heading: QUOTE
sections.text: Whether a catchphrase you repeat constantly or a one-time zinger, your quote sums you up in a single phrase or sentence that ties everything else together. If they ever make a movie about you, the quote is the line everyone’s going to remember long after leaving the theater. Feel free to leave this one blank and come back to it after you’ve played a few games and gotten to know your Hero a little better.

sections.heading: CONNECTIONS
sections.text: Describe at least three people who play an important role in your life. This doesn’t necessarily mean you like these folks, or even know them. It just means they’re connected to you in some way. Connections can include family members, friends, pets, coworkers, rivals, and so on. If you have Perks like Contacts or Patrons, these people don’t count as connections unless they’re important to you on a personal level, in which case you can make them connections if you wish. You don’t have to actually create these Extras, leave that to your GM. Simply describe who they are and how they’re connected to you so the GM can bring these people into the game when they want to make a story personal to you.

sections.heading: DETAILS
sections.text: The second-to-last step is to make up at least three details: one about you, one about one of the other Heroes in the group that somehow relates to you, and one about someone or something out there in the game world that somehow relates to you. You can make up any details you want. They can be related to each other or not. They can involve the past, the present, or the future. They can involve your backstory, your history, or your fate. And whether you or anyone else knows or believes these things to be true is entirely up to you. The only requirement is that each detail must provide the GM with a plot hook that can be used as the basis of a subplot or story. The GM must approve your details, and your fellow player must approve the detail about their Hero. Otherwise, the sky’s the limit.

sections.heading: ORIGIN
sections.text: The last thing to do is describe how you became a superhero. You don’t have to write a novel. In fact, a simple sentence or two that leaves a lot to the imagination can sometimes be more evocative than pages of backstory. And be prepared to read it, because the first thing that should happen once everyone creates their Heroes is that each player should read their origin to the rest of the group. The Heroes may not know one another’s backstories at the start of the game, but the players usually should.

sections.heading: ADVANCEMENT
sections.text: Character advancement is not a major theme of the superhero genre. Most well-known comic book characters are iconic, changing little over time. This reliable sameness is part of their charm, and why they keep getting rebooted every few years. On those rare occasions when superheroes do change, it often comes as a sudden and dramatic transformation rather than slow and steady growth. Despite this, P&P includes rules for character advancement because that’s part of the fun of playing a roleplaying game. Players expect their Heroes to become more capable over time, and there’s a lot to be said for watching your creation go from rookie crime fighter to veteran superhero. As with everything else, feel free to alter or ignore these rules to suit your game.

sections.heading: GAINING HERO POINTS
sections.text: GMs should award each player 1 Hero Point roughly every 3 issues. These points should be awarded after the Heroes complete a story. If your group tends to complete stories in a single issue, you may want to award Hero Points every few stories instead. Each Hero should also receive 1 Hero Point any time they accomplish something truly noteworthy. For example, Heroes who defeat an archvillain or save an entire city (state, country, planet, etc.) from imminent destruction should be awarded an extra Hero Point. In addition to the above, Heroes are awarded 1 Hero Point whenever they experience a major life event like a marriage, the birth of a child, the death of a loved one, or any other important event in their personal life. At least some part of this event must occur in the game rather than off screen. Although these life events are driven by the players, GMs are always free to add whatever potential drama and excitement they wish. Only one Hero can experience a major life event per story, so players are expected to take turns doing this over the course of a series. Occasionally, these events can involve the entire group, like when two Heroes get married and the rest are invited to the wedding. The GM is free to bar major life events from happening in certain issues or stories, as well as to limit how often they can happen at all, thereby dialing the game’s soap opera level up or down as desired.

sections.heading: SPENDING HERO POINTS
sections.text: New Hero Points can be spent to buy new characteristics or improve existing ones. Everything costs the same as during character creation. For example, raising your Might by 1d costs 1 Hero Point, while raising your Super Speed by 1d costs 3 Hero Points. If you raise a Trait that acts as a Power’s baseline rank, that Power increases in rank as well. For example, if you have 3d Might and 9d Strike, raising Might to 4d will raise Strike to 10d because Might is the baseline rank for Strike. Heroes can also spend Hero Points to buy extra Flaws. The first 3 Flaws are always free, so characters with less than 3 can make up the difference without spending Hero Points. The fourth, fifth, and sixth Flaws cost 3 Hero Points each. No Hero can have more than 6 Flaws (unless the GM approves). If you ever grow tired of a Flaw or feel like your Hero has outgrown or overcome it, you can swap it out for a different Flaw between stories. This doesn’t cost Hero Points, but you need to explain how this happened. Players shouldn’t do this too often, though, or Flaws will start to feel meaningless.

sections.heading: TRAIT CAPS
sections.text: Games can have a hard Trait Cap or a floating Trait Cap, as determined by the GM. Hard Trait Caps never change, no matter how many Hero Points the characters earn. Floating Trait Caps, on the other hand, increase over time. Ordinarily, a floating Trait Cap increases by +1d for every 10 Hero Points a Hero earns through advancement. In other words, the game’s Trait Cap increases by +1d once a Hero earns 10 Hero Points, by another +1d once they earn 20 Hero Points, and so on. As an alternative, GMs are free to ignore the above and instead simply increase the game’s floating Trait Cap whenever they think it’s appropriate. In game terms, this might be after the Heroes defeat an archvillain or accomplish a major milestone in the series. In comic book terms, this might be after each Special Issue or Anniversary Issue. However they handle this, GMs always have the absolute right to control the Trait Cap in their games and raise it at whatever speed they wish, if at all.

sections.heading: RETCONS
sections.text: Every so often, players should also be allowed to retcon their Heroes. In the comics, a retcon (short for retroactive continuity) is a dramatic change made to a character or another important element of a series, often one that rewrites established canon to some degree. In P&P, a retcon refers to letting players change their Heroes however they wish. This can run from something as small as swapping a few Ability and Talent ranks to something as large as completely redesigning a Hero from the ground up. As long as the character costs the same number of Hero Points, anything goes during a retcon, subject to the GM’s final approval. As in the comics, retcons can be explained within the story of the game or they can be hand-waved—do whatever works best for your game.

sections.heading: RANDOM HERO GENERATOR
sections.text: If you find yourself at a loss when trying to create a new Hero, see if anything on the following tables sparks your imagination. If that doesn’t do it, roll randomly to see what kind of character develops. Of course, this is just for ideas and inspiration—you aren’t bound by these rolls.

sections.heading: NATURE
sections.text: Your nature describes what kind of being you are. You can select your nature from the following options, or you can roll 2 dice and check the Random Natures table to let fate decide. If you want to make things interesting, roll 3 dice instead of two, making sure the third die is a different color. If you roll a 6 on the third die, it means you have two natures. Pick a second nature or roll a second time (and you may as well add that third die to this roll as well, because why not)

You may be a new arrival to Earth, or you might have travelled here as a baby so that this is the only home you know. If you look human, you might not even know about your alien heritage. The differences between you and ordinary humans may be invisible to the naked eye, little more than cosmetic, or enough to grant you tremendous abilities under our yellow sun. Animal: You are an animal that has somehow become sentient, or maybe you were always that way. You might be an alien, mythic, or unearthly being who happens to be intelligent, or you may have become sentient as a result of whatever event or process granted you your other special abilities. Construct: You are an artificial being like an android, a magical construct, a robot, or a vat-grown human simulacrum. While many constructs are inanimate, many others are as alive as any living creature. Your special abilities are often inherent, part of how you were designed or intended to function. Human: You are an ordinary human being. While you probably come from present-day Earth, you may be from another time, another dimension, or both. Regardless, you are just an ordinary person, or at least you were at some point before you gained or developed your superhuman abilities. Mythic: You are a magical creature or a member of a hidden culture or race like an amazon, centaur, dragon, dwarf, elf, faerie, ghost, ghoul, immortal, merman/mermaid, minotaur, mummy, nymph, ogre, revenant, satyr, troll, vampire, werewolf, or zombie. Plant: You are a sentient, plant-based life form. You may always have been this way, or perhaps the same alteration or enhancement that granted you your special abilities made you sentient as well. At least some of your special abilities are probably the result of your unique physiology. Unearthly: You are a being from another dimension or plane of existence, like an angel, demon, or demigod, or maybe you come from some otherworldly realm where such beings reside. Some or all your special abilities are attributable to your inhuman or extradimensional nature.

sections.heading: BASIC ORIGIN
sections.text: Your basic origin provides a general idea of how you developed your special abilities. Although this may suggest what your special abilities represent (i.e., their Source) you always have the final say and can give your Powers whatever Source you want. You can select your basic origin from the following options, or you can roll 1 die and check the Random Origins table to let fate decide. If you want to make things interesting, roll 2 dice instead of one, making sure the second die is a different color. If you roll a 6 on the second die, it means you have two basic origins. Pick a second one or roll a second time (and while you’re at it go ahead and roll that extra die again as well).

sections.heading: RANDOM ORIGINS — ROLL BASIC ORIGIN
sections.text: 1 Altered 2 Designed 3 Equipped 4 Gifted 5 Inherited 6 Skilled Altered: You were altered or transformed in some way. This might have been the result of a random accident, event, or occurrence, or you may have been intentionally enhanced with biotech, cybernetic implants, experimental gene therapy, magical tattoos, permanent spells, etc. If you are a construct, you were modified or redesigned for something other than your original purpose. Designed: You were created or designed to have your special abilities. This basic origin is most applicable to Constructs, so feel free to select this without rolling if you are a Construct or to reroll this result if you are anything else (although you can make this work for any nature). Equipped: Your special abilities come from one or more objects you acquired or made. These objects might be tools you actually use, like a high-tech suit of powered armor or a magic sword, or they might instead be talismans or sources of power, like a ring charged with cosmic energy. Gifted: You were born with your special abilities, although they may not have developed until later in life. Your abilities are not shared by other members of your race or species; they are unique to you. You are special: blessed or cursed, a genetic anomaly, a mutant, the one, etc. Inherited: You were born with your special abilities or they developed naturally. Your special abilities are shared by other members of your race or species, so you probably aren’t human. But you might be, in which case destiny, fate, prophecy, or a unique bloodline may be the source of your powers. Skilled: Most of your special abilities are the result of intense training, whether physical, mental, or mystical. The rest often represent arms, armor, and equipment you have at your disposal.

sections.heading: SUPER TIP!
sections.text: Your origin isn’t about how you got your powers. It’s about why you’re a superhero. A Hero’s origin is usually what cements their Motivation in place.

sections.heading: SOURCES
sections.text: These are the Sources for your Powers and Abilities with a rank of 7d or greater. Abilities of rank 6d or less are assumed to be Innate, and Talents are assumed to be Trained, regardless of their rank, but these defaults aren’t mandatory. If you select or roll other Sources and would like to apply them to your Abilities and Talents, you are free to do so. Decide how many Sources you want to use, then pick the ones you want or roll one die and check the Random Sources table for each.
